dekaf: Fix missed field folding

Field folding was applied to the `avro::RecordField.name`, but not applied to the avro schema's location itself.

Without the fix, we see a similar error to the one observed in production:
```
running 1 test
test test_field_selection_recommended_fields ... FAILED

successes:

successes:

failures:

---- test_field_selection_recommended_fields stdout ----

thread 'test_field_selection_recommended_fields' panicked at crates/avro/src/schema.rs:251:28:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Invalid schema name root.invoice/additional_charges._items._flow_extra.RawJSON. It must match the regex '^((?P<namespace>([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*(\.[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)*)?)\.)?(?P<name>[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)$'
```

validation: relax check over `explicit_plane` on update

created.

control-plane-api: unconditionally fetch an `explicit_plane_name`

Previously, we fetched only those data-planes named by storage_mappings,
but this is problematic in two ways:

* The ops/ tenant doesn't have storage mapping data-planes, because it
  has tasks / collections across *all* data-planes and has special-case
  handling to allow the publication to proceed.

* If an explicit data-plane is passed to a publication, but that
  data-plane isn't in storage mappings, the result is a confusing "this
  plane doesn't exist" error even if it does, in fact exist.

Update `seed.sql` to remove the ops/ data-plane, making it better mirror
production.

agent: fix controller retries of inferred schema updates

We've observed a bug in prod where a publication to update the inferred schema
fails, but the controller's next attempt is scheduled for ~4 hours out, even
after the first failure.  The issue here was a `.do_not_retry()?` in the
collection controller, which meant that it fell back to the 4 hour periodic
check rather than attempting to re-try.  But the larger issue was that this
behavior was not covered by tests, so I added an integration test for it.

control-plane-api: multiple changes to GraphQL

Makes several changes to the graphql API, some of which are significant breaking changes:

- Fix the graphql uri in the GraphiQL HTML (fixes the query UI)
- Removes the separate `nodes` field from paginated `Connection` type. This
  field seems to be related to the
  [Global Object Identification](https://graphql.org/learn/global-object-identification/)
  pattern, which we do not use. It's added by default by the `async_graphql`
  crate, but this commit disables it.
- Standardize all queries that accept a catalog prefix input to accept a single
  prefix instead of a list of prefixes. The list wasn't useful for the UI, and
  adds complexity to the backend.
- Use pagination on all the top-level stuff that fetches by prefix
    - alerts
    - live specs
    - prefixes
- LiveSpecs
  - Rename separate `captures`, `collections`, etc to just `live_specs`, and enable optional filtering by type
  - rename `spec` -> `model` in response
  - Add isDisabled to response
  - refactor the query input to accept a single prefix, and an optional `catalogType`
- Rename `AuthorizedPrefix` to `Prefix`

Also better organizes the query types using a separate `Query` impl for each
module, which all get merged in `graphql/mod.rs`.

flowctl: move graphql queries from flow-client into flowctl

Moves the query closer to the thing that's using it. The full graphql schema is
still output under the `flow-client` crate, so that it can be used by other
crates besides flowctl.

agent: update error message for auto-discover failures

The message now includes all of the publication errors in the event that the
publication failed. These error messages get used for alerts, so including the
publication errors here is meant to ensure that alert error messages are actionable.

agent: update shard_failed alert error message

Uses the detailed error message from the shard failed event when generating the
alert arguments. This helps the shard failure alerts be more actionable.

models: refactor publication JobStatus

Updates the JobStatus enum into a struct with a separate type enum.  This does
_not_ change the serialization format at all, and the new struct is fully
compatible with all pre-existing serialized statuses.

The previous JobStatus was not able to easily be exposed as a GraphQL type.
This change sets the stage for us to return JobStatuses from GraphQL queries.

control-plane-api: rename LiveSpecs.specType to catalogType

"spec" is sooo 2023

control-plane-api: add status to liveSpecs graphql schema

This adds an graphql query that's roughly equivalent to the `/api/v1/status` endpoint.
I tried a few different ways of exposing the `ControllerStatus` enum via graphql,
before landing on the approach of defining explicit functions for each of the fields
we want to expose. I decided against the graphql `Union` type, because it requires
that clients use conditionals to match agains the type of the status before they can
select the fields that they want. So instead, I just manually defined the schema for
`ControllerStatus` to be a union of the fields that appear in each status type.
There were also some minor changes to some sub-status structs, for example to
replace `serde_json::Map` with the std `BTreeMap`, but apart from that it's
mostly just adding a bunch of derives.

control-plane-api: refactor liveSpecs and add connections

Significantly refactors how live specs are queried and represented
in the graphql schema.

- Introduces the `LiveSpecRef` type, which acts as a reference to a live spec.
- Move additional resolver functions for `firingAlerts`, `alertHistory`, and
  `status` from `LiveSpec` into `LiveSpecRef`.
- Uses the `Snapshot` for resolving top-level queries of `LiveSpecRef`s
- Adds `readsFrom`, `writesTo`, `readBy`, and `writtenBy` resolvers on
  `LiveSpec`s, which return paginated lists of `LiveSpecRef`s
- Unify all dataloader implementations under a single `PgDataLoader` type
control-plane-api: rename 'firing' to 'active' on alerts

control-plane-api: remove generic type from Publisher

This refactors the Publisher to make it easier to test our GraphQL API.  The
issue is that the `App` type is used extensivly by our API handlers, and it
embedded `Publisher<DataPlaneConnectors>`.  This generic type parameter posed
problems for testing, where we need to use `MockConnectors`. This factors out a
`Builder` trait, which can be made into a trait object.  Now, the publisher
embeds an `Arc<dyn Builder>`, and it no longer needs a generic type parameter.

This sets us up to be able to test our graphql handlers by creating an `App`
that has a `Publisher` that uses `MockConnectors`.

control-plane-api: add graphql handler tests

Adds tests for the existing graphql handlers. The test cases are each just a
file containing a graphql query. We run some common setup, and then execute
each query in the context of each of two users and snapshot the results.

Note that these tests are in the `agent` crate because they need to access the
database.  Cargo runs tests for different crates in parallel, which would
otherwise cause tests to step on each other if they were in separate crates.

Also fixes a bug with ControllerStatsus loading for newly published specs.
When specs are first published, they have an empty controller status, and serde
deserialization will fail. This caused graphql queries to fail if the status
was queried before controllers could set it properly. The status DataLoader
impl was updated to use the same behavior as the controllers executor for
deserializing the statuses.  It first checks the `controller_version`, and
returns an Uninitialized status if it is 0.

control-plane-api: fix alert history pagination

Pagination of alerts was broken because it used a plain timestamp as the
cursor, but it's possible for mutliple alerts to all have exactly the same
fired_at timestamp.  This fixes the cursor so that it includes the alert type
and catalog name, and uses all three fields in order to resume at the proper
point in the list.

control-plane-api: Updates to `liveSpecs` graphql query

Updates the graphql handler for `liveSpecs` to fetch the names from the
database instead of using the `Snapshot`. This is done in order to ensure that
newly published specs will show up in the list results.

Adds support for both forward and reverse pagination in both the top-level
`liveSpecs` query, and in all the field resolvers for connected specs (e.g.
`readsFrom`).

Also introduces support for querying live specs by name. To support this, the
query parameters changed from `liveSpec(by: { prefix: "foo/", catalogType:
collection })` to `by: { prefixAndType: { prefix: "foo/", catalogType:
collection}}`. To query by name, you'd use `by: { names: ["foo/a/name"] }`.

control-plane-api: group predicates under `by` in alerts graphql query

Updates the `alerts` query to be consistent with the `by` pattern, to
clearly distinguish pagination parameters and predicates.

control-plane-api: use `by` for predicate in prefixes query

Makes the `prefixes` query consistent with the rest. This query is really kind
of a placeholder, but I figured it can at least be an up-to-date placeholder.

agent integration tests: cleanup handling of Snapshots in tests

Previously, the tests were starting the same snapshot refresh loop that's used
in prod. That didn't make much sense, because tests should always complete well
before the snapshot would need refreshed. And just in general, we'd prefer more
deterministic behavior in tests. So this changes it to just initialize the
snapshot once, upon execution of the first graphql query.

json: major refactoring with AsNode trait migration from doc crate

Migrate AsNode trait and Pointer from doc crate to json crate, enabling
schema validation to work directly with AsNode instead of walking serde
deserializers.

Completely re-implement JSON Schema validation. The new implementation
continues the stack-based, single pass validation done by the prior
validator, but eschews hash-based identity tracking as certain keywords
(like "const", "enum", and "unique") are now able to directly examine
document structure if they need to.

Getting rid of interning and having a single Keyword instance for
Properties / Required, with index tracking as validation progresses, is
a key optimization -- the prior implementation was O(N*N) when
evaluating objects with many properties, all of which were schematized.

A lot of attention has also been paid towards being as L1/2/3 cache
friendly as possible: almost all validation work is done as a single
joint forward pass of the document and the validating schema(s),
with predictable cache access patterns.

Also update to the current draft 2020-12 JSON Schema standard and test
suite, with backward compatibility for "additionalItems" and a few other
keywords. Support for "recursiveRef" and "recursiveAnchor" is dropped
in favor of supporting the newer "dynamicRef" and "dynamicAnchor".

The pre-existing citi_bike and github-based benchmarks show JSON Schema
validation to be about 3x faster. This may undersell the improvement for
many production use cases having large numbers of schematized properties.

- Remove AsNode/Pointer implementations and walker.rs, and update

doc: optimize combiner key comparisons with embedded key prefix

Refactor Meta structure to embed first 13 bytes of extracted key tuple
directly in the metadata. This optimization reduces memory fetches during
sorting and merging operations by allowing most key comparisons to be
resolved using only the cached Meta bytes.

Changes:
- Meta expanded from u32 to 16-byte structure with embedded key prefix
- Keys extracted upfront when documents added to MemTable
- Spill format updated to accommodate larger entry headers (8 → 24 bytes)

Performance improvements come from better CPU cache utilization - most
comparisons avoid fetching full keys from memory. The packed structure's
natural byte ordering aligns with (binding, key) tuple ordering for
efficient inequality tests.

reasonable catalog sizes.

in capture, derivation, and materialization validation paths. Tests verify

dekaf: Fix race condition causing zombie `TaskStateListeners`

The symptoms of this bug are sessions erroring with `Access token has expired and the task manager has been unable to refresh it.` after previously seeing logs about `TaskManager hasn't had any listeners for a while, shutting down`. This indicates that somehow, `TaskManager::get_listener` is handing out `TaskStateListeners` with zombie watch channels. This is a race condition:

1. Task manager times out after `TASK_TIMEOUT`, is about to exit
2. New session arrives and calls `get_listener()`
3. `Receiver` is still prsent in `TaskManager.tasks` hashmap, and since the task manager hasn't dropped its `Arc` yet, `Weak::upgrade()` succeeds
4. New session gets a `TaskStateListener` with the soon-to-be-closed watch channel inside
5. Task mananager finishes shutting down, dropping its sender and closing the watch channel.
6. `TaskStateListener::get()` calls `borrow_and_update()`, which _doesn't care_ that the channel is closed, and hands out the most recently published `TaskState`
7. Since `Session` holds a `TaskStateListener`, which holds a strong `Arc<watch::Receiver<..>>`, so long as at least one Session is alive, all future session will also still get the bad channel since `Weak::upgrade()` will succeed.

Failed to increase partition count for topic ...: Some(TopicAuthorizationFailed)

**Breaking changes:**

This includes some minor breaking changes to flowctl command-line arguments.

The arguments for selecting specs by catalog type now only permit a single
catalog type to be selected.  They also no longer accept explicit boolean
values, so for example `--captures=true` would now be passed as just
`--captures`.

The `--data-plane-name` argument now only accepts a single value, where
previously it could be passed multiple times.

Both of these changes were made because they were infrequently used corners of
the API, and it didn't seem worth the extra code complexity to support them.

Lastly, it is now required that you pass a `--prefix` or `--name` argument if
the current user is authorized to more than 5 different catalog prefixes. This
is because our graphql API requires a prefix selector when listing live specs.
When running `flowctl catalog list|pull-specs` without any `--name` or
`--prefix` argument, flowctl will first fetch a list of the user's authorized
roles. If there are fewer than 5 of them (after removing redundant nested
roles), then it behaves as if the user had passed each of them as a `--prefix`
argument. For the cosmopolitan users with access to more than 5 distinct
prefixes, you'll be required to pass an explicit `--prefix` argument.

There was also a minor non-breaking addition of the `--models` argument,
which enables including the live specs models in the output when using
`--output json|yaml`. This makes it easier to peek at the model without
needing to run `pull-specs` and then clean up all the files.

graphql: combine liveSpecs query predicates into one object

Removes the @oneOf when querying liveSpecs, and combines both name
and prefix predicates into a single object.

The server requires that at least one of `names` or `prefix` must be specified,
because our authorization checks are based on these parameters.  The server
will only return specs that match all predicates in `LiveSpecsBy`.  For
example, if `names` is given along with both `prefix` and `catalogType`, then
it will only return specs matching all three.

This also changes how authorization checks are peformed. Previously, when
querying `liveSpecs` by name, the response would include a result node for each
requested spec, even if the user has no capability to it. Now, if a query
requests a name that the user is not authorized to read, it returns an error
instead, failing the entire request.

This change also revealed a problem with the use of the
`verify_user_authorization` function.  That function would `sleep` if the
authorization check failed, waiting for a refresh before re-checking. During
integration tests, that refresh loop is disabled, so tests would hang
indefinitely. This was resolved by just faking the `taken` timestamp
of the snapshot to be in the future.

graphql: support `startedAt` parameter for non-blocking authZ checks

Resolves #2480

Adds an optional `startedAt` parameter to top-level graphql queries, which
controls the blocking behavior when a request tries to access resources that
the user lacks capability to. Because the `Snapshot` is only updated
periodically, we need to wait until the next snapshot refresh in order to
definitively say that a user lacks a given capability. If `startedAt` is not
provided, then we'll block until the next snapshot refresh in order to be
certain about the authorization decision.  But if `startedAt` is provided, and
the snapshot was last refreshed _before_ `startedAt`, then we'll return an
error response that includes a `retryAfter` extension, which indicates to the
client that it may retry the request in order to get a more definitive answer.
If `startedAt` is provided and the value is _after_ the time of the last
snapshot refresh, then the authorization decision is definitive and no
`retryAfter` will be returned.

agent: generalize publication cooldown

Resolves #2505

Replaces the `INFERRED_SCHEMA_UPDATE_COOLDOWN` with a more general
`CONTROLLER_PUBLICATION_COOLDOWN`, which applies to all controller-initiated
publications. In scenarios where a bunch of collections all have inferred
schema updates in rapid succession, this prevents the connected captures and
materializations from being repeatedly published in response to changes in the
collections. In prod, we've observed that connected tasks are getting published
very frequently during those times, and our goals here are to:

- try to reclaim some system capacity that could be used for publication for other tenants, tasks, etc
- prevent repeated publications from causing too many task restarts, and thus impacting task performance

This ended up requiring a bit of refactoring, particularly in the materialization controller.

The cooldown is implemented as a special error. The `RetryableError` type now
has an `is_backoff` field, which is used to coalesce multiple different backoff
errors into one. This ensures that we have consistent reporting of cooldown
errors, even if a controller makes multiple attempts to publish. The status
summary logic was also updated to ignore these cooldown errors. Generally, a
cooldown error is not a condition that users will care about or be able to act
on.

The `nextUpdateAfter` field from the inferred schema status was deprecated,
and a new `nextAfter` field was added to the publications status. Any time
controllers are waiting on a publication cooldown, they'll set that field
to the timestamp of the next attempt.

agent: prevent restarting failed shards during publication cooldown

Addresses an issue from the previous commit, which introduced generalized
publication cooldowns.  That cooldown interacts poorly with our shard restart
behavior. Our restart behavior is to always restart shards immediately after
the first 2 failures of any particular build (the build changes every time it's
published), and only starts backing off after the 3rd consecutive failure. So
in scenarios where we're waiting on the publication cooldown for a
materialization, we're now doing 2 immediate restarts of a materialization that
is very likely to fail. Restarting failed materialization shards can be pretty
resource intensive for data planes, so it's worth it to avoid doing 2 extra
restarts on materializations. So this augments the shard restart behavior so
that we won't attempt to restart a failed shard if we're awaiting a publication
cooldown. It does this for all task types, even though materializations are the
main ones that are impacted, due to them commonly having a large number of
bindings for collections that use schema inference.

doc: check allocations after every document drained from spill

Previously `alloc` was size checked only if the entire document was successfully
reduced. Schemas with a nested non-associative "last write wins" reduction
strategy (such as history mode captures) do not get reduced because of this, but
allocations may occur prior to the reduction traversing to that nested location
from reducing a top-level merge, for example. This can lead to unbounded memory
growth, and in extreme cases OOMs.

The fix here is to check the allocator size for every document drained.

A benchmark simulating history mode was added to verify that memory usage stays
under the threshold as documents are drained. Prior to this change, memory usage
would continue to grow indefinitely, potentially reaching multiple gigabytes.

agent-api: fix sub-second precision mismatch in agent-api causing incorrect terminal authorization errors

The authorization evaluator compared `snapshot.taken` which contains sub-second precision against the JWT's `iat` claim which only contains second-level precision. This caused the authorization API to return terminal failures when fetching auth within the same second as a snapshot refresh.

Example timeline:
```
> Snapshot fetched at 15:32:44.76
2025-12-18T15:32:44.767374Z INFO control_plane_api::server::snapshot: fetched authorization snapshot collections=8 data_planes=1 migrations=0 role_grants=7 user_grants=4 tasks=7

>  Publication committed at 15:32:44.86
2025-12-18T15:32:44.861475Z INFO try_publish:commit{build_id=13555487ce800352}: control_plane_api::publications: finished publication commit attempt=0 attempt_elapsed_ms=5 commit_elapsed_ms=5 result="success" temp_dashboard_compat="successfully committed publication"

> Task started and attempted to fetch authorization at 15:32:44.98
2025-12-18T15:32:44.981443Z WARN authorize_task: control_plane_api::server::authorize_task: error=status: 412 Precondition Failed, error: task shard capture/test/my-task/source_ingest/13555487ce800352/00000000-00000000 within data-plane local-cluster.dp.estuary-data.com is not known
```

The comparison `snapshot.taken > started` evaluated as: `15:32:44.763 > 15:32:44.000 = TRUE` (terminal failure)

But the snapshot (taken at `.763`) was actually OLDER than the request (`.981`).

The fix is to truncate `snapshot.taken` to seconds when comparing.

dekaf: Map binding backfill counter to Kafka leader epoch for collection reset

When a collection is reset or a materialization binding is backfilled, consumers
need to detect that their committed offsets are invalid. This maps the binding's
backfill counter to Kafka's leader epoch mechanism:

* Emit `leader_epoch` in Metadata and ListOffsets responses
* Validate consumer epoch in Fetch and ListOffsets, returning `FENCED_LEADER_EPOCH`
  for stale epochs and `UNKNOWN_LEADER_EPOCH` for future epochs
* Implement `OffsetForLeaderEpoch` API - returns offset 0 for old epochs (reset to
  beginning) and current high watermark for current epoch
* Append `-e{counter}` suffix to upstream topic names for offset isolation by epoch

Also isolate committed offsets by task name and clean up legacy offsets.
Previously, all topics sharing the same token would commit offsets to the same
upstream Kafka topic name, creating potential conflicts across tasks/tenants.

* Swap encryption nonce from token to task_name when epoch suffix is present
* Clean up oldoffsets after successful epoch-qualified commit, only after the new commit succeeds
dekaf: start at epoch 1, not 0.

dekaf: Include `UnknownTopicOrPartition` in list of retryable errors

This shows up sometimes, I believe attributed to eventual consistency in

dekaf: Update read logic to bubble up `JournalNotFound` into `UnknownTopicOrPartition`
dekaf: Only send a `committed_leader_epoch` if the partition has committed offsets

Fix Cloud Run deployments after Dockerfile relocation (#2558)

* Fix Cloud Run deployments after Dockerfile relocation

Dockerfiles were moved to docker/ directory in commit fec63eca6f as part
of the mise infrastructure refactoring, but deployment workflows were
never updated.

The new Dockerfiles expect binaries in architecture-specific subdirectories
(${TARGETARCH}/), but workflows were copying binaries directly to crate
directories.

Fixed workflows:
- deploy-agent-api.yaml: Create amd64/ subdir, copy agent and sops
- deploy-data-plane-controller.yaml: Create amd64/ subdir, copy binary, entrypoint, and sops
- deploy-oidc-discovery-server.yaml: Create amd64/ subdir, copy binary and entrypoint

Each workflow now:
1. Creates amd64/ subdirectory in the source location
2. Copies the built binary into amd64/
3. Copies required scripts (entrypoint, sops) into amd64/
4. Copies the Dockerfile from docker/ to the source directory
5. Cloud Run deployment proceeds with correct directory structure

Verified locally that Docker builds succeed with this structure.

This fixes Cloud Run deployments that have been broken since December 1st.
Discovered when #2549 triggered the data-plane-controller deployment.

* Deploy pre-built images from Platform Build instead of building from scratch

Refactors deployment workflows to use pre-built Docker images from Platform Build CI
rather than rebuilding from source on every deployment, as suggested by Johnny.

Benefits:
- Faster deployments (no build step)
- Deploy exactly what was tested in CI
- More efficient resource usage
- Simpler workflows (39 net lines removed)

Changes:
- data-plane-controller: Triggers on Platform Build completion, deploys pre-built image
- oidc-discovery-server: Triggers on Platform Build completion, deploys pre-built image
- agent-api: Manual trigger only, deploys pre-built dev-next image

All workflows now:
1. Determine the image tag (from Platform Build or dev-next for manual triggers)
2. Deploy the pre-built image from ghcr.io/estuary/{service}:{tag}
3. Skip all build/package/Docker build steps

Images are built by Platform Build workflow via mise/tasks/ci/docker-images which:
- Builds all docker/*.Dockerfile images as multi-arch (amd64/arm64)
- Pushes to ghcr.io/estuary/ with git describe tags
- Runs automatically on every master branch push

* Use Artifact Registry proxy for ghcr.io images

Cloud Run cannot pull directly from external registries like ghcr.io.
Instead, it requires using Artifact Registry remote repositories which
act as a proxy to the external registry.

Updated all deployment workflows to use the Artifact Registry proxy path:
  us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/estuary-control/ghcr/estuary/{service}:{tag}

The remote repository was created with:
  gcloud artifacts repositories create ghcr \
    --project=estuary-control \
    --repository-format=docker \
    --location=us-central1 \
    --mode=remote-repository \
    --remote-docker-repo=https://ghcr.io

Platform Build continues pushing to ghcr.io, and Artifact Registry
automatically proxies pulls from Cloud Run to the upstream registry.

* Add fetch-depth: 0 for git describe to find tags

Without fetch-depth: 0, actions/checkout does a shallow clone that
doesn't include tags. This causes git describe --tags to fall back
to just the commit hash instead of the proper version tag.

Added to deploy-data-plane-controller and deploy-oidc-discovery-server
workflows which use git describe to determine the image tag.

The deploy-agent-api workflow doesn't need this since it hardcodes
TAG="dev-next".

Introduce notifications crate

Adds a rust crate for rendering notification messages using handlebars
templates. This will be used by the new alert system for rendering alert
emails.

The previous alerts edge function used the `mjml-browser` library
to style the base alert templates so that they match the visual style
of the application UI. This removes that in favor plain HTML, which
was generated by an LLM from the original mjml template. The resulting

control-plane: alerts redux migration

Adds a database migration for moving to the new alerts system.

This migration disables the previous alerting system by disabling the
evaluation cron job, and disabling the triggers on `alert_history`.

The new alerts system has an automations task for each alert, which gets
created when the alert is fired, and which cleans itself up
automatically after resolution emails are sent.

The migration adds a new `id` column to `alert_history`, in order to
associate each alert with the notification automation tasks. The
`task_id` of the notifications task is the same as the `id` of the
alert. Technically, this column could have been named
`notification_task_id`. But it also happens to function as a surrogate
id, since there is at most 1 notification task per alert, and the
notification tasks need to be able to query alerts by this id. So I'm
kinda just leaning into that, and calling it `id`. This doesn't replace
the unique index on `(catalog_name, alert_type, fired_at)` (though we
might one day revisit that index).

control-plane: complete alerts migration

Disables the old alerting system and enables the new one, completing the
cutover.

agent: Introduce alert evaluation and notification

Adds end-to-end alerting to the agent. Previously, alerting was handled
by a postgres cron job, which would evaluate alert views, add/update
`alert_history`, and send email notifications via the alerts edge
function. This adds all of that functionality to the agent, along with
a number of improvements.

The new system is able to tolerate faults in both sending notifications
and in alert evaluation, so we should no longer have problems with
missing alert emails. And any alerts tht get fired by controllers will
no longer suffer from a delay due to the cron-based evaluation.

The `agent::alerts` module documentation has an overview of how the main
pieces fit together, so I won't repeat that here.

During development and testing, I stumbled across some problems that
were ultimately caused by cloning the `models::IdGenerator`, causing
duplicate ids to be generated. So I removed the `Clone` impl from
`IdGenerator`, so it's no longer a footgun.

Fix deployment workflows to use Platform Build commit SHA (#2596)

* Fix deployment workflows to use Platform Build commit SHA

The deployment workflows were failing because they checked out the
current HEAD of master, which could be ahead of the commit that
Platform Build just finished building. This caused git describe to
generate a tag for a newer commit, and the image pull would fail
because that tag doesn't exist in the registry yet.

Fixed by using github.event.workflow_run.head_sha to checkout the
exact commit that triggered Platform Build. This ensures git describe
runs against the same commit Platform Build used, generating matching
tags.

For manual workflow_dispatch triggers, falls back to github.sha since
workflow_run context doesn't exist.

Changed workflows:
- deploy-data-plane-controller.yaml
- deploy-oidc-discovery-server.yaml

* Fix agent-api deployment to use git describe instead of dev-next

The agent-api workflow was failing because it tried to deploy a
'dev-next' tag that doesn't exist. Platform Build only pushes version
tags from git describe (e.g., v0.6.0-116-gbc1bb91ac8), not dev-next.

Changed agent-api workflow to:
- Add fetch-depth: 0 to checkout
- Use git describe --tags --always to get the actual version tag
- Deploy the image that Platform Build actually pushed

This allows manual deployments to deploy whatever commit is checked out,
as long as Platform Build has already built and pushed that version.

agent: allow pausing sending alert notifications

Introduces a `--serve-alert-notifications` argument, to allow us to
disable the execution of the alert notifications automation, while still
serving other types of background automations. This gives us a way to
effectively pause and resume the sending of alert notifications.
Previously, we'd only had the ability to leave `--resend-api-key` unset,
but doing that would still execute the alert notifications jobs, so
there was no way to resume where we left off.

agent: fix argument parsing for emails

Fixes a bug in the argument parsing when enabling sending of alert
notifications. The group was incorrect, as it would permit at most one
argument in the group. Replaces it with just two separate requires.

agent-api: set container CMD

Hopefully this will fix our cloud-run deployments for agent-api.
Cloudrun expects the image to have an implicit entrypoint or command
set, and we were just using plain `bash`. So this sets the container
`CMD` to the entrypoint script that works for `agent-api` in cloud-run.
This same image can still be used to deploy `agent` in k8s, because
we already override the `command` in that environment.

json: validate all occurrences of duplicate object properties

Previously, when a document had duplicate property names (e.g.,
`{"foo": 1, "foo": 2}`), only the first occurrence was validated
against the schema's `properties.foo`. Subsequent duplicates were
treated as additional/unevaluated properties.

Fix by using a peekable iterator to look ahead at the next property.
The counter is only incremented when processing the last occurrence
of a duplicate, allowing all occurrences to match against the same
schema property.

dekaf: handle collections with no journals by returning retryable Kafka errors

It's possible for a collection to exist in the control plane without having
any extant journals. This can happen either when the capture task is failing or
hasn't emitted any documents, and more frequently during a collection reset.
Previously, Dekaf treated this the same as a missing collection, causing
consumers to receive non-retryable errors or inconsistent behavior.

Introduces `CollectionStatus` enum to distinguish three states:

* `Ready`: binding exists and journals are available
* `NotFound`: binding doesn't exist in the materialization spec
* `NotReady`: binding exists but journals aren't available yet

For `NotReady`, we'll use `LeaderNotAvailable` (a retryable error) to cause
consumers to retry with backoff until the journals become available.
They will eventually give up.

Previous to #2566, Dekaf would always use TLS when talking to upstream brokers. When we introduced support for non-TLS connections (for e2e testing) by interpreting the URI scheme, I forgot about `connect_to_group_coordinator` and `connect_to_controller` which need to be made aware of the configured URI in order to work properly.

Now,

dekaf: remove buggy `decode_safe_name` call from `authenticate()`

Task names containing periods (e.g. `foo.com/tenant/task`) were being corrupted during authentication. The issue: `decode_safe_name()` replaces `.` with `%` then attempts percent-decoding, so `foo.com` becomes `foo%com`, and `%co` is invalid hex, leaving the name corrupted.

The `decode_safe_name` function was added in #1516 to support dot-encoded JSON config objects as usernames (e.g. `{}` encoded for platforms that don't allow `{` in usernames). When materialization task-based auth was introduced in #1665, the dot-encoding was never removed despite no longer having a valid use case: users provide task names via SASL auth username which doesn't have the same limitations as topic names.

This PR removes the `decode_safe_name()` call from `authenticate()`. It's still used by `from_downstream_topic_name` for decoding Kafka topic names in order to avoid breaking backwards compatibility.

rocksdb: fix batched merge to preserve null deletion markers

Only the first batch of each iteration should use `full` reduction,
since it contains the base value. Subsequent batches contain only
operands and must use associative (partial) reduction to preserve
null deletion markers in merge-patch schemas. Previously all batches
used the caller's `full` flag, causing LWW delete to strip null
markers within non-first batches instead of preserving them for
re-merge with the base.

adds a targeted regression test, and a QuickCheck fuzz test that
verifies batched merges match json_patch::merge at various batch sizes.

agent: introduce background publication alerts

Adds a new alert type called `background_publication_failed`. This alert
fires after controllers make 3 consecutive failed attempts at publishing
a live spec. That condition is intentionally broad, so that it covers
many different failure scenarios, such as:

- inferred schema updates
- source capture updates
- config updates
- periodic publications
- catalog test failure

Note that auto-discover publications will _not_ trigger this alert,
since the auto-discover alert is more targeted.

The alert resolves after any successful publication.

The config update controller was also updated to have an incremental
backoff, so that the alert doesn't take so long to fire.

renames it to `Message`, to set up for a later commit to add
republishing support.

postgres: enable tcp keepalives

This is meant to address an issue that's been observed a few times with our
stats-view materialization.  Those incidents happened due to the connector
exiting unexpectedly in the middle of sending a batch of updates to the
database.  When that happens, the other timeouts like
`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`, `statement_timeout`, `idle_timeout`,
etc. do not take effect because the session is not considered "idle" when it is
in "ClientRead" state. Therefore, the only way for the server to detect the
disconnected client and terminate the session (which may still be holding
locks) is by using tcp keepalive probes.

In [RFC1122](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122#page-101), it explicitly
states that the _minimum_ default keepalive interval is 2 hours, in order to
maintain compatibility with systems that don't support keepalive at all. That
means that it will take _at least_ 2 hours before the database server will
terminate the session after a client unexpected disconnects in the middle of
sending a batch, which is far too long for our purposes.  Two hours surely made
sense in 1989, but today keepalives are almost universally supported, at least
in our domain. So it seems prudent to lower the idle interval to allow much
faster detection of broken connections.

validation: add tests for key with write-schema default vs inferred additionalProperties: false

Demonstrates the bug where adding a key field (/_meta/store) that has a
default value in the write schema fails validation with "location is
prohibited from ever existing" when the inferred schema's parent object
has additionalProperties: false.

The root cause is in Shape intersection during allOf composition: the
inferred schema's additionalProperties: false imputes a false schema for
properties not yet observed, and intersecting with the write schema's
property shape produces type_: INVALID. intersect_default() then drops
the default because its type doesn't overlap with INVALID, and locate()
coerces Exists::May -> Exists::Cannot, causing walk_ptr() to raise
PtrCannotExist.

Includes both a simple write schema case and a $ref chain case matching
the source-shopify-native connector structure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

doc, validation: treat default as annotation in schema intersection

Relaxes intersect_default() to treat `default` as a pure annotation
(like `title`, `description`, `reduce`) rather than re-validating it
against the intersected type. The intersection now simply takes
lhs.default.or(rhs.default) without checking type overlap.

This is safe because defaults are already validated locally against
their containing schema during inference. The previous behavior was
too strict: when an allOf intersection produced type INVALID (e.g.,
from additionalProperties: false in the inferred schema), it would
drop the default even though it was valid in its originating schema.

In walk_ptr(), adds `&& default.is_none()` guards to the Cannot-exist
checks so that a location with a default bypasses the PtrCannotExist
error. When read_exists is Cannot (but has a default), skips read-side
key checks (type, reduce, redact) since the INVALID shape is not
meaningful for validation.

Fixes the source-shopify-native scenario where /_meta/store has a
write-schema default but the inferred schema hasn't observed it yet.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.6 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

avro: treat null default as nullable for Avro schema generation

When `default` is preserved as an annotation through schema intersection
(from the prior commit), a field with `default: null` and intersected
type `integer` was incorrectly mapped to a non-nullable Avro `Long`.
The nullable check used `shape.default.is_none()`, which returned false
for `Some(null)`, skipping the union with Null.

A null default is equivalent to no default for nullability purposes:
the field can be absent and absence maps to null.

validation: use effective_type union for key checks instead of skipping

Addresses review feedback: instead of wrapping reduce/redact/keyable
checks in `if read_exists != Exists::Cannot` (which skips them entirely),
compute an effective_type as the union of read_shape.type_ and the
default value's projected type. This preserves all key validation checks
(type, reduce, redact) while allowing the keyable check to pass when the
default itself is a keyable type.

Also uses effective_type for the read/write type comparison so it
correctly matches the write schema type when the read location Cannot
exist but has a default.

control-plane-api: enforce strict $defs check in update_connector_schema

The legacy migration path in update_connector_schema silently replaced
any existing schema that didn't mention flow://connector-schema with a
new {$ref: flow://connector-schema} wrapper. This was intended to
migrate old collections into the managed-schema pattern, but that
migration is long complete. Keeping it is a liability: if a user

initialize a read schema under the connector's direction — changes

gazette: always use routing topology in client, remove proxy-conditional routing

Production Gazette deployments don't use a reverse proxy, and the
client-side behavior of ignoring known topology when `do_not_proxy`
wasn't set was counterproductive: there are requests (like metadata
fetches) where you want a peer to forward on your behalf for reduced
latency, while still using the response's route on a subsequent
request.

If a reverse proxy setup were reintroduced, the proxy itself would be
responsible for rewriting response headers to reference itself rather
than the internal brokers it fronts.

Concretely:
- Append, Fragments, and Read always use topology-aware routing
  (Primary or Replica as appropriate) instead of falling back to
  Mode::Default when `do_not_proxy` is unset.
- In read_some, capture metadata response routing before branching,
  fixing a gap where the fragment-URL path lost routing info.
- Re-pick a routed subclient before starting a direct journal read,
  so the data stream is served by a broker that actually serves the
  journal rather than the arbitrary default dialed for metadata.

dekaf: add missing timeout to `fetch_partitions()` in task manager loop

`fetch_partitions()` calls `journal_client.list()`. This was the only network call in the task manager loop not wrapped with a timeout. If the RPC hangs for whatever reason, the task manager loop blocks permanently, the published access token expires, and all sessions get "Access token has expired and the task manager has been unable to refresh it." indefinitely.
dekaf: add logging around errors or panics to `run_task_manager`

dekaf: reap abandoned reads that are no longer being fetched by the consumer

Dekaf holds a PendingRead (and its backing Gazette Read RPC) for each topic/partition a consumer has fetched. Previously, the only cleanup path for these reads was inside the Fetch request handler, which ran only when the consumer sent a new Fetch for that specific partition. If a consumer stopped fetching a partition while keeping its connection alive, the PendingRead and its open gRPC stream persisted indefinitely.

These abandoned streams accumulate unconsumed data, exhaust the HTTP/2 connection-level flow control window on the Gazette broker connection, and block all response traffic on that connection including List RPC responses needed to resolve partition info.

Add a periodic reaper in the connection handler that drops any PendingRead whose last_accessed timestamp exceeds STALE_READ_TIMEOUT (default 1m).

Remove the old 5-minute fetch-level read expiry, which is no longer needed.

agent: discovers update disabled collections

Makes some subtle but important changes to how discovers and
auto-discovers handle updates to collections for disabled bindings.
It's common for users to start with a binding that's enabled, and then
disable it later, then re-enable, etc. This presents a challenge in
several scenarios. The most acute and timely, issue is that our control
plane needs to keep collection specs up to date with respect to the
current discover and publish behavior. This is especially important
in scenarios where a user subsequntly re-enables a binding.

This changes `prune_unchanged_specs` so that it no longer prunes specs
for bindings that are disabled. Instead, controller-initiated
publications now use the `PruneUnboundCollections` publication finalizer
in order to avoid publishing collections that meet both the following
criteria:

- The drafted collection represents an insert (no existing live spec)
- The capture binding is disabled (the collection is 'unbound')

It also unifies the behavior of user-initiated and controller-initiated
discovers. Previously, a user-initiated discover would update these
collections, while an auto-discover would not because of
`PruneUnboundCollections`.

The way that added and modified bindings are counted in the discover
outcome was cleaned up a bit, so that we can avoid counting collections
as modified when the binding is disabled.

dekaf: cap per-partition fetch reads with a configurable combined limit

Dekaf placed no upper bound on how much data it buffered per Fetch
request. A consumer could send large `partition_max_bytes` values across
many partitions and cause unbounded memory growth.

This adds a `--combined-partition-fetch-limit` / `COMBINED_PARTITION_FETCH_LIMIT`
config (default 50MB) that caps the total bytes read across all partitions
in a Fetch. The limit is divided evenly across all fetched partitions, and
each partition's read target is capped at
`min(partition_max_bytes, limit / num_partitions)`.

* `fetch.max_bytes` from the client remains ignored because it is meant
  as an after-the-fact cap on response size, not a pre-flight allocation.
  Dividing it across partitions would starve active partitions when most
  partitions in the request are idle, which is a common pattern when
  consumers subscribe to many partitions but only a few have data.
* `max_wait_ms` is not capped since bounded bytes prevent resource
  overcommit regardless of wait duration
* Adds `dekaf_fetch_partition_bytes` histogram to track the actual byte
  size of each partition's fetch response

shuffle: top-level crate README and wiring, plus Frontier and Binding

`Binding` represents extracted shuffle configuration for a single binding
of a task.

Frontier is a delta of progress available for consumption.
It's closely related to the existing Gazette checkpoint concept,
but additionally represents "causal" hints that are tracked and resolved
internal to the shuffle protocol.

shuffle::session: RPC for overall shuffle session management

The Session RPC is the entrypoint of a distributed shuffle.

It spawns and coordinates subordinate Slice RPCs, assigns journals to
slices for reading, and aggregates & reports available progress
upwards to the coordinator client.

shuffle::slice: scale-out first stage of distributed shuffles

Slices are a scale-out RPC (one per member) which do the heavy lifting
of monitoring journal listings and reading across assigned journals.

They sequence documents across their assigned journals, track producer
states, and route & enqueue documents to Queue RPCs. They initiate flush
barriers which allow the Slice to report deltas of progress upwards to
the Session.

Each Slice RPC maintains a Queue RPC to each member queue (MxM fan-out).

shuffle::queue: scale-out second stage of distributed shuffles

Queue RPCs join across and receive Enqueue and Flush requests from Slice
RPCs. They merge and order recieved Enqueues, write to an on-disk queue
file (still TODO), and respond to Slice Flush barriers.

Queues build out the on-disk queued state which will be dequeued from
using the checkpoint presented to the shuffle coordinator by the session
RPC.

agent: detect and disable abandoned tasks

Adds two alert sequences that identify tasks that are persistently failing or not processing data, and progressively disable them.

* Sequence 1 fires `TaskChronicallyFailing` when `ShardFailed` has been continuously active for 30+ days with no user publication in 14 days, then fires `TaskAutoDisabledFailing` after a 7-day grace period.
* Sequence 2 fires `TaskIdle` when a task has moved no data for 30+ days with no recent user publication, then fires `TaskAutoDisabledIdle` after 7 days. Idle detection is suppressed while failure alerts are active so users receive only one notification path.

The controller now tracks `last_data_movement_ts` (from `catalog_stats_daily`) and `last_user_pub_at` (most recent non-system-user publication) to evaluate both sequences.
A user publication resets a 14-day suppression window before alerts can fire. All thresholds are configurable via environment variables, with disabling of tasks disabled by default

tokens: select on drop signal during Source::refresh()

The watch() background task only checked its drop signal in the outer
select! loop, not while blocked inside source.refresh(). For
StreamSource-backed watches (like partition list_watch), refresh()
blocks on the gRPC stream waiting for the next broker response. When
all PendingWatch clones were dropped, the task stayed stuck in
refresh(), keeping the gRPC connection open indefinitely.

This prevented gazette brokers from completing graceful shutdown —
they'd wait for the lingering list_watch RPC to end, eventually
logging "grpc.GracefulStop took too long" and issuing a hard Stop
(~15s delay in e2e tests).

Wrapping the refresh() call in a select! with the drop signal lets
the task exit immediately when all watchers are gone, closing the
gRPC stream and allowing brokers to shut down promptly.

Also add PendingWatch::into_parts().

proto-gazette: tighten uuid::sequence() "deep rollback"

Previously, any commit clock which was less-than the last commit clock
was considered a "deep rollback". Turns out this is too restrictive,
because various read restart scenarios have only lower-bound resumption
journal offsets. We must read and filter through previously-read
portions of the journal, which means we may see stale ACKs.

Instead, only consider a stale ACK to be a deep rollback if we've seen
CONTINUE_TXN documents at clocks greater than the last_commit clock.
This scenario cannot occur during re-reads of previously-read journal
content.

shuffle: add block encoding format for on-disk log

Implement a columnar block format for efficiently storing batches of

or the 65k block-per-segment limit. Blocks above a size threshold
are LZ4-compressed before writing (though in practice, this is either
usize::MAX for "off" or zero for "on").

SealedSegment manages rolled segment files: after a delay it
compresses them in the background, then polls for reader completion
before unlinking. Yields reclaimed bytes as a stream for the actor's
disk backlog tracking.

shuffle: add log reader with frontier-driven scanning

Implement the read path for consuming committed entries from the
on-disk log. Reader manages segment file open/close with lazy
initialization and monotonic LSN watermarks.

FrontierScan provides the high-level iteration interface: it tracks
remainder blocks (partially consumed), maintains a clock index for
efficient resume, and yields only entries committed relative to the
current Frontier. BlockScan iterates committed entries within a
single block using binary search on an index of clock visibility.

Segment handles low-level file I/O with read_at() for random access
and automatic unlink-on-drop cleanup.

waking blocked response channels, and draining the append heap with
disk backlog back-pressure.

shuffle: filter stale causal hints using per-cohort completed clocks

When a binding is re-enabled, its journals catch up from behind the
cohort frontier, emitting ACK documents with causal hints referencing
commits the cohort already completed. These stale hints would block the
checkpoint pipeline and eventually trigger the mark-and-sweep timeout.

unresolved from the constructor.

graphql: add basic connector queries

Adds some basic graphql schema for querying information about connectors
and connector tags. The graphql schema aligns pretty closely with the
current data model of the `connectors` and `connector_tags` tables. This
was done to try to ease the transition from postgresT.

There's a bit of awkwardness with that data model, because listing
connectors involves filtering by protocol, which is only known
for connector _tags_ that have had at least one succesful Spec
performed. This turns out to be not a big deal because, for our only use
cases for listing connectors, we only need to return connectors that
have had at least one successful spec performed. In other words, we only
want to list connectors that have an associated `endpointSpecSchema` and
`resourceSpecSchema`, since those are the only ones that can be used by
the UI.

There's still a use case for returning information about connectors that
_haven't_ had a successful spec RPC, though. For example, a connector
developer will want to create/update a connector tag, and would need
visibility in cases where the spec RPC fails, so they can troubleshoot.
So the singular `connector` resolver will always return a connector, and
all the associated tags, even when some or all of the Spec RPCs have
failed.

The internationalized text in connector titles, descriptions, etc, is
exposed only in the translated form. A `Locale` was added to `Envelope`,
and is intended to be pushed down into database queries where
appropriate. At the moment, connectors are the only api that will use
this, but it seemed like the right approach to determine locale based on
the request, and so this just moves us toward that.

Querying connector tags can be done in two ways. You can either query
for a connector, and use the `connectorTag` resolver, or you can use the
top-level `conectorTag` resolver, which accepts a full image name and
returns either the tag matching the version of the image, or the default
tag. While we normally try to avoid adding extra graphql schema when
it's not necessary, in this case the separate resolver adds relatively
little code, and the flexibility seemed helpful for UI development.

flowctl: always encrypt all endpoint configs

Resolves #2709

Previously, flowctl's endpoint encryption logic would skip over any
tasks that used connector images or tags that aren't represented in the
`connector_tags` table of the
control plane database. This commit makes two changes:

- If the image tag is not known, but there's another tag for the same
  image, then we'll use the endpoint config schema from that other tag
  to perform the encryption
- If there's no usable `connector_tags` row for that image name, then
  error and abort the publish, discover, etc.

As part of that, the encryption module was updated to use the new
graphql api for resolving the connector schemas. This allows it to
easily request the specific tag used by the task, or fallback to the
default tag for the connector image.

graphql/connectors: expose `defaultCaptureInterval` and make `filter` optional

Adds `defaultCaptureInterval` to `ConnectorTag`, sourced from the existing `connector_tags.default_capture_interval` column, so the UI can populate the polling interval for non-streaming capture connectors.

Also makes the `connectors` query callable without a filter: both the top-level `filter` argument and `ConnectorsFilter.protocol` become optional, and the SQL `where` clauses skip the protocol predicate when no filter is supplied. Previously callers listing all connectors had to pass a protocol filter.

graphql/connectors: rework API surface to hide multi-tag internals

The connector_tags table is an implementation detail that consumers of the GraphQL API shouldn't need to know about. The API now presents connectors as a catalog with a single blessed version per connector, and a resolver for fetching the spec of any specific version.

* Rename `ConnectorTag` to `ConnectorSpec` and remove internal fields (`id`, `connectorId`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`) that exposed the DB schema. The type now contains only what's needed to configure a connector: `imageTag`, `protocol`, `endpointSpecSchema`, `resourceSpecSchema`, `documentationUrl`, `disableBackfill`, `defaultCaptureInterval`.

* Remove `Connector.tags: [ConnectorTagRef!]!` and the `ConnectorTagRef` type from the public schema. The multi-tag list is still loaded internally for default-tag resolution but is no longer a GraphQL field.

* Replace `Connector.connectorTag(imageTag, orDefault)` with two fields: `spec(imageTag!)` for exact version lookup and `defaultSpec` for the blessed tag. Add `Connector.protocol` derived from the default tag so consumers can categorize connectors without resolving a spec.

* Replace the top-level `connectorTag(fullImageName, id)` query with `connectorSpec(fullImageName!)`. It tries the exact tag and falls back to the default if not available; the returned `imageTag` tells the caller which version was actually resolved.

* Update flowctl's endpoint config encryption to use the new `connectorSpec` query. The always-encrypt behavior is unchanged.

* Fix `PaginatedConnectors::new` argument order: `has_previous_page` and `has_next_page` were swapped.

* Fix protocol filter to use an EXISTS subquery so the filter controls which connectors appear without affecting which versions are aggregated internally. Add missing `filter(where ...)` clause on `array_agg` in backward pagination.

* Remove duplicate `Locale` enum from graphql/mod.rs (the real one lives in envelope.rs).

* add test coverage for spec(), error paths, and missing fields

* `spec(imageTag)` returning a non-null `ConnectorSpec` (previously only tested returning null for missing/failed tags)
* `documentationUrl` and `defaultCaptureInterval` fields on `ConnectorSpec`
* `connectorSpec(fullImageName)` with no tag delimiter (error)
* `connector()` with no parameters (error)
* Unauthenticated request (error)

graphql/connectors: re-expose ConnectorSpec.id as deprecated

The UI's config-encryption edge function, discovers flow, and secrets management all still reference connector_tags rows by ID. The previous commit removed this field since ConnectorSpec isn't conceptually a database row, but these downstream consumers aren't ready to migrate away from it yet. Re-add the field with a GraphQL deprecation annotation so it remains available while signaling that it will be removed.

graphql/connectors: add `recommended` filter to ConnectorsFilter

The `Connector` type exposes `recommended: Boolean!` but `ConnectorsFilter` only supported filtering by `protocol`. This adds an optional `recommended` boolean filter so callers can request only recommended (or non-recommended) connectors without client-side filtering.

* Add `recommended: Option<bool>` to `ConnectorsFilter` and both pagination SQL queries
* Update one test fixture connector to `recommended = true` and add test cases for both filter values

control-plane(alerts): add prefix-scoped `alert_configs` for per-task alert tuning

Alert thresholds lived in incompatible places: agent env vars (`ALERT_AFTER_SHARD_FAILURES`, `CHRONICALLY_FAILING_THRESHOLD`, `IDLE_THRESHOLD`, `DISABLE_*_TASKS`) for everything except `DataMovementStalled`, which used the `alert_data_processing` side table. Enabling `shardFailed` or auto-disable defaults fleet-wide was blocked because any single global value was wrong for some subset of tasks, and no per-prefix override existed. RFC #2845 Phase 1 introduces `alert_configs`, a prefix-or-name keyed table read by the agent during alert evaluation:

* `alert_configs.config` carries per-alert-type subconfigs (`dataMovementStalled`, `shardFailed`, `taskChronicallyFailing`, `taskIdle`) and `autoDisable.{idle, failing}` toggles. Longest-prefix-match with exact-name override selects the effective row; absent fields fall through to `ControllerConfig` env defaults.
* `DataMovementStalled` evaluation moves into the per-task controller pipeline, retiring the `AlertEvaluator<DataMovementStalledAlerts>` automation and the `alert_data_movement_stalled` view. The effective `AlertConfig` is fetched once at the start of each controller run and passed to the `activation`, `abandon`, and `data_movement` evaluators.
* `alert_configs` is accessed exclusively through the `alertConfigs` query and `updateAlertConfig` mutation; writes require admin capability on the governing prefix. `alert_data_processing` is unchanged and continues to accept UI writes; the controller consults it as a fallback only when no `alert_configs` row supplies a `dataMovementStalled.threshold`. A follow-up data migration will copy remaining rows into `alert_configs` after the UI has switched to the GraphQL mutation.

flowctl(alerts): add `configs` subcommand and group under top-level `alerts` The `alert_configs` GraphQL surface introduced in the previous commit had no client. flowctl is the first consumer so operators can manage rows during the `ShardFailed` opt-in rollout and so the GraphQL surface is exercised end-to-end before UI work begins. The existing `alert-subscriptions` is folded under the same top-level command: * `flowctl alerts configs list [--prefix

]` paginates the `alertConfigs` query (the first paginated GraphQL command in flowctl) and renders rows with the standard `--output {table,json,yaml}` selection. * `flowctl alerts configs set ` accepts either `--set foo.bar=value` / `--unset foo.bar` for read-modify-write patches, or `--config ` for whole-row replace from YAML or JSON. Patch values are JSON-parsed when possible (so `true`, `42`, `"30d"` work) and fall through to strings otherwise. Both modes deserialize the merged JSON through `models::AlertConfig` before the round-trip so `deny_unknown_fields` surfaces typos client-side. * `flowctl alert-subscriptions` is moved under `flowctl alerts subscriptions` and retained as a hidden top-level alias for backwards compatibility. Existing scripts continue to work; the alias is no longer surfaced in `--help`.

agent(alerts): gate task auto-disable strictly per-prefix

Auto-disabling abandoned tasks is opt-in per prefix or task via `alert_configs.{taskIdle, taskChronicallyFailing}.autoDisable`, defaulting off. With `alert_configs` as the configuration surface for every other alert knob, folding auto-disable into the same model keeps two invariants: a per-task `autoDisable: false` can never be overridden by a global setting, and `TaskAutoDisabledFailing` / `TaskAutoDisabledIdle` fire only when a task is actually disabled, so the alert's message ("task auto-disabled after ...") is always true at fire time.

* `autoDisable` defaults `false` and is set via `alert_configs.{taskIdle, taskChronicallyFailing}.autoDisable`.
* `TaskAutoDisabled*` alerts fire only when the task's shards are disabled by the controller.

doc: add ExtractorPlan with merge-join field extraction

Pre-compiles a Vec<Extractor> into blocks: runs of consecutive
sibling-leaf extractors under a common parent. Each block walks to
the parent once and merge-joins the parent's fields against the
block's leaf names, replacing N root-to-leaf Pointer::query + N
Fields::get with one walk and a linear sweep.

Singletons stay on the reference path — block setup has no advantage
over Fields::get for a single lookup. Output bytes are identical to
the reference path; a differential fuzz follows.
doc: add ExtractorPlan differential fuzz test

doc: add ExtractorPlan vs Extractor perf benchmark

Six shapes spanning the happy path (wide flat block), the risk case
(sparse block in a large parent), and the no-op case (no blocks) —
the win ranges from ~0x (no-blocks) to ~5x (deeply nested).
runtime: use ExtractorPlan for materialize value extraction

doc: document ExtractorPlan tiebreak on duplicate object keys

HeapNode preserves duplicate JSON object properties (raw bytes through
serde_json::Deserializer keep them; only serde_json::Value coalesces via
BTreeMap).

Field extraction is a pick-one operation, and the pre-refactor reference
path was already implementation-defined on duplicates: Fields::get uses
a linear find() (first match) below 16 fields and binary_search_by
(arbitrary match) at or above. The ExtractorPlan merge-join always
returns the first match, so it agrees with the reference below the
threshold and can disagree at or above it.

This test pins down the divergence with a minimal, deterministic
construction: a 3-field parent where both paths agree, and a 16-field
parent where binary_search_by lands on the second duplicate while the
merge-join stays on the first. It also asserts the plan's output is
independent of parent size, documenting "first occurrence wins" as the
plan's defined tiebreak unless Fields::get is made deterministic too.

docs: warn that conditional reductions need `required` on the discriminator (#2917)

JSON Schema's `properties` keyword only constrains a property when it
is present, so `properties: { foo: { const: "X" } }` matches docs where
`foo == "X"` *and* docs where `foo` is absent. In a tagged-union
reduction this silently routes every document missing the discriminator
down the wrong branch — most damagingly, a delete-by-`_meta/op` rule
without `required` stanzas converts every reduced document into a
delete and drops it from the destination.

generalization to `oneOf`/`anyOf`. Update the existing `oneOf` example
to declare `required: [action]` on each branch so the canonical example
models the safe pattern.

validation/collection: catch non-functional and fragile redact placements

Redaction is applied at capture time using the write schema, and `$defs/flow://*` subtrees are owned by the system (overwritten by discover or by validation-time inlining). Annotations placed only in the read schema, or anywhere inside a `flow://*` subtree, are accepted today even though they produce no protection at all (read-only) or are erased on the next publication (managed defs). At least one production incident required retroactively deleting unredacted customer data because of a misplaced annotation.

* `ReadSchemaRedactNotInWriteSchema`: errors for any `redact` whose pointer has no corresponding `redact` in the write schema; otherwise captured documents reach storage unredacted regardless of what the materialization does on read.
* `RedactInsideManagedDefs`: scans the user-authored model for `redact` annotations inside `$defs/flow://...` and reports the offending JSON pointer; reads the pre-inlining model so verbatim copies of the write schema that validation inlines into `$defs/flow://write-schema` are not misreported.

Closes #2914.

validation: cascade backfill on collection reset regardless of onIncompatibleSchemaChange (#2916)

When a user resets a capture or collection, the validation layer detects the reset via partition template name changes and applies the binding's `onIncompatibleSchemaChange` setting. For `disableBinding` and `disableTask`, this silently stopped data flow with no error in the UI. The fix: when `was_reset` is true, always increment `model.backfill`. `Abort` is preserved (it surfaces a visible error). The `group_by_changed` and field-selection paths are unchanged.

A user resets their capture expecting data to start flowing fresh. Instead, a downstream materialization with `onIncompatibleSchemaChange: disableBinding` silently goes dead. The setting was designed for system-detected schema incompatibilities, not user-initiated resets.

authz: introduce capability bundle authorization model

Authorization grants confer a set of named bundles (Viewer, Writer, Editor, Admin, Billing, TeamAdmin, Delegate, Assume) stored in a new `bundles` array column. Application code maps each bundle to a set of fine-grained capability bits, and authorization checks operate on those bits:

* The bundle-to-bits mapping is an application-layer concern, so new capability bits can be introduced or recomposed in code without a DB migration.
* A single `reachable_nodes` BFS evaluates authorization over `authz::CapabilitySet`; `Delegate` and `Assume` bits express transitivity explicitly, rather than hard-coding propagation when `capability == Admin`.
* `Capability::None` (renamed from the placeholder `x_00`) supports grants whose authorization comes entirely from the bundles column, so roles like `Billing` can be granted without leaking `read` access through RLS.
* A new `OrthogonalCapability` GraphQL enum and `PrefixRef.capabilities` field expose the fine-grained bits to clients, allowing future feature gates to check specific capabilities rather than coarse legacy levels.
* The legacy `capability` column continues to drive RLS unchanged; `bits_for_legacy` converts existing `read`/`write`/`admin` values to bundle-equivalent bit sets so existing authorization callers compile and behave identically for current grants.

billing: split `invoices_ext` data view from authorization wrapper

`public.invoices_ext`'s `authorized_tenants` CTE materializes the full `tenants` table for any role with `rolbypassrls`, and its LATERAL preview branch runs `generate_series` and `billing_report_202308` across every materialized tenant. The GraphQL resolver's parameterized `WHERE billed_prefix = $1` did not push through the CTE, so `tenant.invoices` hangs. Extract the data logic into `internal.invoices_ext` (no auth) and query it directly from the resolver, which already runs `verify_authorization`:

* `billed_prefix = $1` pushes through `UNION ALL` into each branch's tenant predicate; preview's `tenants` scan becomes a single-row index lookup.
* `invoiceType` filters cause the planner to prune the preview and manual branches entirely.

`public.invoices_ext` is rewritten as a thin join over the internal view; `billing-integrations/publish.rs` and the pgTAP suite behave identically.

    Connectors must publish all documents before a terminal `more = false`.
  - Response.Opened gains runtime_checkpoint, promoted from the internal

runtime-next: fix materialize idempotent-replay recovery livelock

On recovery of a prepared-but-uncommitted transaction, `handler::serve`
builds the first HeadIdle with `idempotent_replay = true` and empty
extents. The recovered hints arrive in the pending `ready_frontier`, but
the close policy reads `unresolved_hints` from `extents.frontier` — empty
until a frontier is applied. So the first tick yields `may_extend = false`
(replay suppresses policy-driven extend, and no extents hints force it):
the recovered frontier is never applied, the txn can neither open nor
close, and the Actor re-steps Idle forever.

Treat an unstarted replay as itself an unresolved hint, forcing the first
extend through the existing close-policy path. Once the recovered frontier
lands in extents, its real hints drive the policy until they resolve and
the replay txn closes.

Fold a regression case into the happy-path FSM test by making its first txn
an idempotent replay rather than a standalone test.

`derive-image-tag` flag overrides the tag (e.g. `local`); otherwise

runtime-next: tab-delimit connector state-patch wire format

The State-Update-Wire-Format framed connector merge patches with `\n`,
but image connectors (derive-typescript/python) read requests as
newline-delimited JSON via `readLines`. A Flush request's embedded
`statePatches` array therefore split across lines, and the connector's
`JSON.parse` aborted with "Expected ',' or ']' after array element",
crashing every built-in TypeScript/Python V2 derivation once non-empty
state flowed (in both the reactor and `preview-next`).

Switch the patch delimiter from `\n` to `\t`: a tab never appears raw in
compact JSON (control chars are escaped inside strings and there is no
insignificant whitespace) yet is still valid JSON whitespace between
array elements, so the payload survives the connector's line framing and
parses directly.

shuffle: prevent flushed_lsn regression across ready/peek paths

The previous floor was stored in `self.ready.flushed_lsn` and applied only
when emitting a fully-resolved ready checkpoint. A peek sourced from
`unresolved` bypassed that floor, so it could carry a lower `flushed_lsn`
than a ready already emitted to the client—causing the Reader to see a
regressing `set_flushed_lsn`.

Introduces `emitted_flushed_lsn` as a dedicated monotonic floor that
`floor_flushed_lsn()` advances on every emission (both ready and peek),
guaranteeing element-wise non-regression regardless of which path fires.

non-tailing) to make head-of-line-blocking visible: a non-tailing read
in `pending_reads` blocks heap drain until all pending reads tail.

`park_or_process` consolidates the entry path: it first tries to resolve
a read immediately via `now_or_never` (skipping a park if data is already
buffered), then classifies the read as tailing or stalled before parking it.
`on_pending_read_resolved` performs the exactly-inverted de-classification
on resolution, eliminating the scattered `tailing_reads` adjustments
that were previously duplicated across every error and terminal path.

new `shuffle_slice_stalled_reads` gauge so operators can observe which
journals are blocking and for how long.

yielding divergent id-sets per transaction during backfill.

(journal, producer) to the *other* cohort bindings reading that
journal, holding checkpoint visibility until all have read through

locate-bin: don't resolve a sibling directory as the binary

`locate()` joined the binary name onto the running program's directory
and used `Path::exists()` to decide whether to use it or fall back to

sharing the binary's name (e.g. a `go/` source tree next to the program)
was canonicalized and returned in place of the real `go` executable.

missing paths. Factor the resolution policy into a private `locate_inner`

runtime: drain shuffle topology on graceful leader shutdown

A back-pressured shuffle Log RPC could wedge graceful shutdown. When a
Log engages disk back-pressure it stops draining a Slice's Appends, which
parks that Slice's request stream so the Log no longer polls it and never
observes its EOF. On shutdown the back-pressure never releases on its own
(nothing is consuming the local log to reclaim segments), so the Log — and
the Session/Slice actors draining it, and the leader awaiting them — hang,
leaking tasks, fds, and on-disk segments.

Break the wedge by relieving the back-pressure out-of-band, reusing the
existing sealed-segment reclaim path:

- shuffle: add `log::remove_shard_segments`, which unlinks a shard's
  segment files (scoped to the `mem-{idx:03}-seg-*.flog` naming; sibling
  shards and `.compress-*` temp files untouched; missing dir / per-file
  NotFound tolerated). The co-located Log's reclaim observes the unlinks,
  drops its backlog below threshold, and resumes draining to EOF.
- shuffle: split `SessionClient::next_checkpoint` into a sync
  `request_checkpoint` + cancel-safe `recv_checkpoint`, letting the leader
  own the SessionClient directly (instead of via `stream::unfold`) so it
  can `close()` it.
- runtime-next leaders: after broadcasting L:Stopped, synchronously
  `SessionClient::close()` — blocking until the whole topology drains —
  before EOFing shards. Intentionally un-timed: a Session that never
  drains is a liveness bug to surface, not mask.
- runtime-next shards: on L:Stopped (a transaction boundary, so we're
  idle and own the shuffle Reader), remove our segment files before
  awaiting leader EOF.

shuffle: fix false-stall on journals last written before not_before

A binding written to in the past but not since its configured `not_before`
was misclassified as a stalled journal. The slice probed the journal's
write head (at offset -1, without `begin_mod_time`) and then started a
blocking read with `begin_mod_time` wired in. The broker filters every
fragment older than `begin_mod_time` and, finding no covering fragment at
or after the fast-forwarded offset, blocks indefinitely under `block=true`
— so the read never resolved and the journal looked stalled, when in fact
it was caught up.

Probe at the checkpoint offset with `begin_mod_time` set (non-blocking,
metadata-only) instead. The broker fast-forwards over filtered fragments
and returns, in a single metadata response, both the offset it advanced to
and the current write head. `start_offset == write_head` then means the
read is caught up; we begin the real read there and classify it as tailing
rather than stalled. Starting at the fast-forwarded offset is safe (the
skipped range precedes `begin_mod_time` and would be filtered regardless)
and keeps the bytes_read / bytes_behind deltas accurate.

Supporting changes:

- gazette read_some: generalize the "caught up" condition from
  `req.offset == -1 || req.offset == metadata.write_head` to
  `metadata.offset == metadata.write_head`. This subsumes both prior forms
  and adds the `begin_mod_time` fast-forward-to-head case, which would
  otherwise fall through to a spurious non-transient error + retry.

- probe_read_start retries on OFFSET_NOT_YET_AVAILABLE. When a reassigned
  broker's tracked end offset transiently lags our checkpoint offset, the
  probe waits for it to catch up — restoring the robustness the old
  offset=-1 probe had implicitly (a blocking read would have waited too).

- ReadState: split `resuming(offset)` into `recovered()` (producer state
  from the checkpoint) and `start_at(offset)` (the offset baseline, seeded
  once the probe resolves), since the starting offset isn't known until the
  async probe completes.

flowctl: migrate to flow-client-next and a live user-token watch

Replace the legacy `flow-client` Client with `flow-client-next` plus the
`tokens` crate. CliContext now carries a PostgREST client, an agent REST
client, a live auto-refreshing `tokens::PendingWatch<UserToken>`, and a
shared gazette Router, applying the user's bearer token per-request.

Token handling is reworked around the watch:
- `UserTokenSource::may_create` gates minting a refresh token from a bare
  access token. It is true only for `auth login` / `auth token`; every
  other context surfaces a bare access token as-is and lets it expire,
  so we never strand abandoned refresh tokens on the control-plane.
- `FLOW_AUTH_TOKEN` is used but never persisted, and is rejected when
  establishing credentials (it would otherwise shadow them next run).
- Startup bootstraps the watch and persists the result; a background
  observer persists each rotation as it happens, so single-use refresh
  tokens can't lock the user out. The observer is awaited before the
  final config write, serializing the two writers.

authorization sources with the shared user-token watch to build
