gazette: only mint pre-signed fragment URLs when actively polled

read() looped straight from one fragment into the next read_some, whose
metadata RPC may mint a pre-signed fragment URL with a short (~60s) TTL. A
consumer that then parked the read before the GET ran let the URL expire,
so the GET failed non-retryably (GCS returns 400 for an expired V2
signature) and the read failed.

Yield before re-entering read_some so its metadata RPC, and thus any
pre-signed URL, fires only once we're polled again — when the consumer is
actually ready to pull the next fragment — keeping the sign-to-GET window
inside a single active read.

models(private_links): move types from data-plane-controller and add async-graphql derives

The GraphQL API and the data-plane controller need to speak the same `PrivateLink` shape: DPC reads the `private_links json[]` column off `data_planes` and ships it into the est-dry-dock Pulumi stack, and the GraphQL surface needs both typed read and a typed input for the mutation that replaces the column. Defining the types once in `models` is the only way to share them without making DPC depend on the GraphQL crate.

* Move `PrivateLink`, `AWSPrivateLink`, `AzurePrivateLink`, `GCPPrivateServiceConnect` to `models::private_links`, re-export from `data-plane-controller::shared::stack` so existing DPC callers keep compiling unchanged.
* Add async-graphql derives under the existing `async-graphql` feature: `Union` + `OneofObject` on `PrivateLink`, `SimpleObject` + `InputObject` on each provider struct. Same Rust enum drives `union PrivateLink` on output and `input PrivateLinkInput @oneOf` on input, so the two GraphQL surfaces cannot drift.
* Azure `dns_name` and `resource_type` flip from `String`-with-empty-as-sentinel to `Option<String>` with a serde adapter that normalizes both an absent field and an empty string to `None` on read and omits both `None` and `Some("")` on write. Wire format byte-for-byte unchanged; the GraphQL surface exposes them as nullable instead of requiring clients to know the empty-string convention.
* AWS `service_region: Option<String>` carries the master-side change (commit b1d51ed2) into the moved type, with `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` so the column stays absent (not `null`) when unset, preserving est-dry-dock's existing fallback to `region`.

control-plane-api(graphql/data_planes): typed `privateLinks` field and `updateDataPlanePrivateLinks` mutation

Exposes the configured private-link endpoints on the `dataPlanes` query as a typed union against `models::PrivateLink`, alongside the three provisioning-result endpoint columns (`awsLinkEndpoints`, `azureLinkEndpoints`, `gcpPscEndpoints`) as opaque JSON arrays. Adds a mutation that replaces the entire `private_links` column on a private data plane; the data-plane controller picks up the new configuration on its next poll and converges via Pulumi.

* `dataPlanes` selects the raw `private_links` JSON once per page and parses each entry lazily in a `ComplexObject` resolver, so a malformed historical row produces a descriptive field-level error naming the data plane and the failing index rather than breaking the whole query selection.
* `updateDataPlanePrivateLinks(dataPlaneName, privateLinks)` accepts `[PrivateLinkInput!]!` directly against the same `models::PrivateLink` types via async-graphql's `@oneOf` input; supplying multiple branches in a single element is rejected by GraphQL validation before the handler runs.
* Name gating is a structural check: the name must sit under `ops/dp/private/<tenant>/...`. Anything more specific (cluster suffix shape, owning prefix shape) is the data plane's problem; an unknown name falls out as "not found" when the UPDATE matches zero rows. Per-provider validation is intentionally not duplicated here: the authoritative schema is the est-dry-dock Pydantic model on the consumer side, and a bad shape surfaces via DPC convergence.
* Interim authorization requires `read` on the private data-plane name, mirroring the existing deployment mutation shape. This will move to `manage_dataplane` once the orthogonal capability model lands.
* Returns `Boolean!` so the mutation surface is minimal; callers that need the post-write state re-query `dataPlanes`.

authz: `ManageDataPlane` bundle gates `dataPlanes` private-networking

Adds two capability bits, `ViewDataPlanePrivateNetworking` and `ModifyDataPlanePrivateNetworking`, composed by a new `ManageDataPlane` bundle. The bundle is granted on the role-grant edge `<tenant>/ -> ops/dp/private/<tenant>/` at provisioning time, so tenant admins (whose `Admin` bundle composes `ManageDataPlane`) inherit both bits on their private data planes; non-admin tenant grantees intersect to their own bundle at the edge and never reach these bits.

* `private_links` resolver on `DataPlane` returns an empty list to callers that lack `ViewDataPlanePrivateNetworking` on the data plane name.
* `updateDataPlanePrivateLinks` mutation requires `ModifyDataPlanePrivateNetworking` (replacing the interim legacy `read` check).
* `evaluate_names_authorization` accepts any `Into<CapabilitySet> + Display + Copy`, letting call sites pass either legacy `models::Capability` or a single `models::authz::Capability` bit; legacy callers keep working unchanged via the `From<legacy>` impl.
* `models::authz::Capability` gets a `Display` impl that delegates to `Debug`, so error messages reference each bit by its Rust identifier.
* `create_data_plane.rs` stamps `bundles = '{manage_data_plane}'` on the new role grant. The accompanying two-step migration adds the enum value and backfills existing rows -- `alter type add value` cannot be used in the same transaction that subsequently references the new value.

oidc-discovery-server: survive direct VPC egress cold-start on deploy (#3062)

On Cloud Run with direct VPC egress, a fresh instance's network interface
takes ~20-40s to begin passing outbound traffic. oidc-discovery-server opens
its database connection at startup and binds its port only after, with a 30s
pool acquire timeout, so when warmup exceeds 30s the process exits before
binding, the startup probe fails, and the revision is rejected.

Raise acquire_timeout to 120s so the pool keeps retrying until egress is ready,
then connects and binds normally. Because the port is bound only after the
connection succeeds, Cloud Run does not route to a not-yet-ready instance, so
this also avoids failed requests on scale-up/scale-from-zero. Add
--min-instances=1 to keep one warm instance serving while others warm up.

runtime/container: use ops::decode::Decoder for log lines

`ops::decode::Decoder` transmutes log lines into ones that are
compatible with our ops logs schema, inferring as much as it can from
the source log when it isn't well-formed and ensuring it has all the
required fields we need.

This is already used in `connector-init`, and that path covers
everything coming from the connector process itself. But it misses
logs emitted by the container runtime, and although these are rare,
they are not in conformance with the ops logs schema and are not valid
logs collection documents.

There is no separate schema validation check of documents written to
logs journals, so it's really important that what we write there is
valid per the schema.

This does duplicate the `decoder` work done in `connector-init`, and
that may be an area for future optimization.

ops/decode: strip only a real trailing newline from raw lines

`rawline_to_log` sliced off each line's last byte, assuming it was a
trailing newline. The final line at EOF may lack one, so this dropped
its last character; worse, the byte-index slice could split a
multi-byte UTF-8 character and panic.

This path is newly reached now that container stderr is decoded here,
where startup and crash diagnostics often end without a newline. Use
`strip_suffix` to remove only a real trailing newline; the existing
`trim_end()` still handles a carriage return or trailing whitespace.
data-plane-controller: remove restart flag (#3087)

runtime-next: durably seed initial connector state as {} to match V1

Connector state is only updated via RocksDB Merge, and the merge operator
treats the first operand on an absent key as the base document -- where a
JSON null is a literal value, not a deletion. So a task first published on
Runtime-V2 stores a connector's first checkpoint of e.g. {"stateKey": null}
verbatim instead of reducing it to {}, corrupting its state from the first
patch onward.

Mirror V1's load_connector_state: when the recovery scan finds no connector
state, durably seed {} as the base and reflect it in the recovered Recover,
so the first checkpoint reduces as a genuine merge patch. Seed only on the
state-bearing shard -- the capture shard, or shard zero of a derivation or
materialization, whose state the leader broadcasts to peers; other shards
must recover an empty Recover.

This replaces a non_empty_state helper that substituted {} only on the
connector-facing Open/Apply requests: it changed what the connector saw, not
what the runtime stored, so the mis-store still happened.

runtime-next: don't abandon the final capture transaction on connector EOF

The capture HeadFSM stepped straight to `Head::Stop` when it observed
connector EOF with no open transaction, without checking whether the Tail
had finished committing. Because a sweep's final transaction is rotated
into the Tail in the iteration just before EOF is observed, the actor loop
(`while !Head::Stop`) could exit with that transaction still mid-commit —
abandoning its documents (no WriteIntents) and its connector checkpoint
(no committing Persist). Each restart then re-swept and re-dropped the same
final batch.

This is V2-specific: exit-after-sweep makes connector EOF the normal
session-end path. It was intermittent because `restart = session_start +
interval` masked it — a sweep finishing faster than the poll interval took
the Sleep arm and the Tail committed during the wait. Only sweeps running
longer than the interval hit the immediate-Stop arm and lost data.

Guard the EOF Stop on `tail_done`, mirroring the sibling `stopping` branch.
When the Tail is still committing, `ready` is Eof so the extend guard can't
match, and we fall through to hold Idle until the Tail reaches Done.

shuffle: make the shuffle disk limit configurable per-task

The shuffle Log actor engages back-pressure once its aggregate on-disk
backlog of sealed segment files crosses a limit. That limit was a single
Service-wide value (2 GiB) applied uniformly to every task served by a
runtime-sidecar.

Expose it per-task via `shards.shuffleDiskLimit` (bytes) in the task model.
The value is carried as a data-plane label `estuary.dev/shuffle-disk-limit` on
the shard spec, decoded into `ops.ShardLabeling`, threaded through the
runtime-next leader into a new `shuffle.Shard.shuffle_disk_limit_bytes` field,
and consumed by the Log handler -- falling back to the Service-wide default
when a task doesn't set it. Only runtime-next materializations and derivations
shuffle; captures carry the label harmlessly but never use it.

The Service-wide default lives in `DEFAULT_SHUFFLE_DISK_LIMIT_BYTES`, exposed
by the runtime-sidecar as the `--shuffle-disk-limit-bytes` flag /
`SHUFFLE_DISK_LIMIT_BYTES` env (both previously named `disk-backlog-threshold`;
renamed since nothing deployed references them yet). The `disk_backlog_bytes`
gauge / `shuffle_log_disk_backlog_bytes` metric are left as-is: they measure
the live backlog, not the limit.

The `_bytes` suffix marks the bare-integer carriers (proto fields, Service /

agent-api: survive direct VPC egress cold-start on instance startup (#3109)

A fresh Cloud Run instance with direct VPC egress passes no outbound
traffic for roughly 20-80 seconds after start. The agent opened its
database pool with connect_with() under the pool's 5-second
acquire_timeout, so every instance started during that warmup window
timed out and exited(1), crash-looping until the interface came up.

Worse, the API port was bound at the top of async_main, so Cloud Run's
default TCP startup probe passed instantly and traffic was routed to
instances that then died: deploys shifted 100% of traffic onto a
revision whose instances all failed, surfacing as "the request failed
because the instance could not start successfully" 500s.

- Create the pool with connect_lazy_with() and retry the initial
  acquire against a 120-second deadline. The pool's acquire_timeout
  stays at 5 seconds: unlike oidc-discovery-server (#3062), it also
  bounds request-path acquires at runtime and must remain short.
- Bind the API port only after the database connection succeeds, so
  the startup probe gates traffic on actual readiness.

gazette: retry Append flow-control underflow instead of hard-failing

A broker aborts an Append RPC when its client can't sustain the minimum
data rate (gazette's MinAppendRate flow-control policing), shedding a slow
or contended client so others may proceed over the exclusively-owned,
highly-contended append pipeline. The append rolls back cleanly and is
safe to retry — indeed gazette's own Go AppendService retries it
indefinitely with backoff.

Gazette surfaces this as ErrFlowControlUnderflow: a bare error that leaves
the resolved status OK, so the client sees it as a gRPC status with code
Unknown and message "append stream: client stream didn't sustain the
minimum append data rate" rather than an AppendResponse.Status.

`Error::is_transient()` only treated Unknown-coded statuses as transient
for two hardcoded transport strings, so runtime-next's publisher (which
gates retries on is_transient) latched it as terminal and failed the
shard. Classify the underflow as transient so it rides the existing retry
+ backoff loop in journal::Client::append, matching legacy behavior.

Verified against a live broker: a deliberately-stalled append is aborted
with the underflow, classified transient, retried, and commits — where
before it hard-failed.

runtime-next: fix materialize 60s tear-down stall

The materialize leader FSM returned `Action::Idle` when reaching a clean
transaction boundary while stopping (both `HeadIdle` and
`HeadStartCommit`). `Idle` parks the actor loop for a full 60s
`ACTOR_TICK_INTERVAL` before it re-polls and notices `Head::Stop`, so
tear-down hung for a minute awaiting the tick.

Return `Action::PollAgain` instead, which the actor loop maps to
`Duration::ZERO` and re-polls immediately, exiting `while !Head::Stop`
without delay. This matches the capture / derive sibling FSMs, which already
return `(PollAgain, Head::Stop)` at their stop boundaries.

runtime-next: factor host seams into Publisher / Shuffle / Logger factories

Factor runtime-next's host-specific behavior — how a task publishes, shuffles,
and logs — out of the crate into three uniform, monomorphized host seams, each a
factory the leader and shard `Service`s are generic over:

- publish: replace the `Publisher` enum — a `Real` variant plus a `Preview`
  variant that baked NDJSON-to-stdout output into the crate — with a
  `PublisherFactory` / `JournalPublisher(Factory)` seam. The publisher now
  carries only document output; its former observation calls move to the Logger
  seam.
- leader: factor the leader's inline shuffle-`Session` opening and checkpoint
  sourcing into a new `leader/shuffle.rs`, providing `ShuffleSession` /
  `ShuffleSessionFactory` (static RPITIT, not `dyn`) plus a
  `ShuffleServiceFactory`.
- log: new `Logger` / `LoggerFactory` seam — the task's out-of-band log and
  event stream. A `Logger` sinks both the connector's own logs (`log`) and
  structured runtime `LogEvent`s (`event`): a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum
  (persist / applied / inferred-schema / container lifecycle) whose variants
  carry borrowed, verbatim payloads so a host may intercept them structurally.
  Its canonical `LogEvent::to_log` flattens each event into the ops-log line it
  replaced, and `event` defaults to that flattening — so a host overrides only
  to intercept, delegating the rest. Production shards install `FnLoggerFactory`
  (sinking to the task-log writer); leaders and tests install
  `TracingLoggerFactory`.

Remove the now-unnecessary `Task.preview` flag from the runtime proto
(reserving field 2): how a task publishes and logs is a host concern decided by
the installed factories, not a protocol flag. `max_transactions` stays as the
transaction bound, re-documented as a general preview/harness control rather
than tied to the removed flag. Make the `shard::rocksdb` module public —
exposing `RocksDB` (with its `open`, `scan`, and now-public
`put_connector_state_base`) and re-exporting its `DecodeError` — so a host
harness can seed shard zero's RocksDB by path and read back its final reduced
state itself, and re-expose `shuffle::log::BlockMeta` for harness segment
writers.

- log: a `PreviewLoggerFactory` sinks the task's log stream and powers

local: per-checkout stack identity, lifecycle & environment

Lay the foundation for isolated per-checkout stacks: every checkout
(primary clone or linked git worktree) gets its own stack identity, and
mise becomes the mandatory entry point that makes that identity ambient.

- stack-env allocates a per-checkout identity — name = sanitized basename,
  index = lowest free slot in 0..15 — in a flock-guarded, machine-global
  registry (stacks.tsv). It derives this stack's ports (base(i) =
  10000 + 1000*i; the last three digits identify the service uniformly)
  and exports FLOW_* / CARGO_TARGET_DIR / GOBIN / DATABASE_URL ambiently
  via mise `[[env]] _.source`, putting built binaries on PATH via a serial
  `_.path` directive. There is no canonical stack.
- lib.sh holds the shared shell helpers; the old `common` task is removed.
- stack / stop / stack-release manage the lifecycle: stop scopes teardown
  to one stack, and stack-release frees the registry slot and reclaims the
  stack's footprint — build artifacts (tens of GB under CARGO_TARGET_DIR),
  the Supabase Docker volumes `supabase stop` preserves, and the private
  state dir — each rm guarded so a short value can't escalate to a shared
  root. stack-info surfaces this checkout's ports, units, and commands.
- DATABASE_URL is exported per-stack (sqlx's compile-time query! macros
  connect to it), so .cargo/config.toml drops its static localhost:5432
  default, which no longer matches any stack.
- Cargo.toml disables incremental compilation: sccache won't cache
  incremental compiles (workspace crates would bypass the shared cache),
  and the incremental/ dir dominates each stack's target-dir footprint
  while sharing nothing across checkouts.

With each checkout owning a stack identity and ambient environment, wire

- systemd user units become templates (flow-*@.service) instanced on the

- supabase/config.toml resolves project id, ports, and site URL through

- build tasks and vm/port-forward, and the local helper scripts and

local: compressed, deduplicated btrfs filesystem for ~/cargo-target

Per-checkout target dirs are 20-60G each and overlap heavily across
checkouts. Back ~/cargo-target on dev VMs with a sparse loopback btrfs
image (50% of disk, capping physical post-compression bytes):

- zstd:3 transparent compression (~3.2x measured on real artifacts)
- a 10-minute duperemove + fstrim timer collapses shared extents and
  punches freed space back into the sparse image (~26% of logical bytes
  deduped even across divergent branches; near-total for same-commit
  worktrees, extent-level dedupe shares blocks of differing files too)
- loop device uses direct-io, via a systemd oneshot unit rather than
  fstab, which cannot express it

bootstrap:cargo-target-fs is idempotent, Linux-only, and never migrates
an existing plain-dir ~/cargo-target (VMs are disposable; recreate to
adopt). vm:create-post invokes it before anything builds.

GOCACHE moves under ~/cargo-target so the large Go build cache lands on
the filesystem; Go stores it uncompressed, so btrfs's single pass does
real work on it. SCCACHE_DIR is deliberately left at its default: sccache
already compresses its own entries, so a compressed blob would only be
recompressed for ~no gain under the compress-force mount (which can't be
told to skip an already-compressed subtree). CI is unaffected: it uses
sccache's GHA backend, and no workflow caches the Go path.

local: reclaim stack slots by deleting the checkout, not a release task

The single signal that frees a stack's slot and artifacts is now that its
registered checkout directory is gone. Being *stopped* releases nothing: a
stopped-but-present checkout keeps its index and its (tens-of-GB) build cache, so
restarting is instant. You release a stack by deleting its worktree; a garbage
collector then reclaims it in the background.

Replaces the explicit `local:stack-release` task with:

- reap-lib.sh: shared reaper sourced by stack-env, stack, stop, and the new
  stack-prune task. reap_teardown_stack tears a stack down by name alone (its
  checkout is gone, so nothing is ambient) — stopping orphaned units first so a

runtime: fix recursive read-lock deadlock in capture-v2 buildJoin

captureAppV2.buildJoin held KS.Mu.RLock and then called shard.Spec()
several times. Gazette's shard.Spec() re-acquires s.resolved.RLock,
which aliases the same KS.Mu. When the Etcd watcher's KeySpace.Apply
writer queued between the outer and recursive read locks, sync.RWMutex
(which blocks new readers once a writer waits) deadlocked: the recursive
RLock could not proceed past the queued writer, and the writer could not
proceed until the outer RLock released at buildJoin's return. That
stalled the keyspace lock for every subsequent reader, parking tens of
thousands of goroutines in a production reactor.

Read from the term's already-captured shardSpec and labels instead of
calling shard.Spec() under the lock. This mirrors buildLeaderfulJoin,
which the derive and materialize V2 paths already use, and is also more
correct: the term is a coherent topology snapshot rather than a
possibly-newer spec read mid-session.

runtime: let docker atomically assign published connector host ports

`start()` probed for a free host port by binding and immediately
releasing a listener, then asking docker to publish that port. Between
the release and docker's own bind, another starting container could
claim the port — for example via its own `--publish-all` — failing
`docker run` with "port is already allocated" and permanently failing
the shard. `flowctl-go test` starts ~40 connector containers
concurrently, making this a recurring CI flake.

Instead, publish with an empty host port, which docker resolves to a
free ephemeral port atomically as the container starts. The mapping is
already discovered from `docker inspect` after startup, so nothing
needed the port ahead of time.

Verified against podman (4.9.3) as well as docker: the assigned port
is reported through `.NetworkSettings.Ports` with the empty `HostIp`
that `inspect_container_network` already handles.

runtime-next: discard hinted frontier when committed frontier is rebuilt

When the materialization leader rebuilds a task's committed frontier from an
authoritative recovered checkpoint — a legacy V1 checkpoint during a V1->V2
migration, or a remote-authoritative connector checkpoint — the recovered
hinted frontier may reference producers the rebuilt committed frontier no
longer carries.

`project_hinted` zeroes each hinted producer's read offset and relies on a
matching committed-frontier producer to restore it. An orphaned hint (no
committed counterpart) therefore resumes at journal offset 0, forcing a full
re-read of the journal from the beginning to replay a hint whose data the
authoritative checkpoint already reflects. On large journals this can prevent
startup from completing.

Discard the recovered hinted frontier whenever the committed frontier is
rebuilt: an authoritative checkpoint is a complete committed frontier, so there
is nothing to replay. Also clear the hinted frontier from RocksDB via the
startup cleanup Persist so it cannot resurface on a later recovery.

Additionally, extract the startup recovery reconciliation into a pure
`reconcile_recovered` function (no IO) and add unit tests covering the discard
on both rebuild branches, hint preservation when there is no rebuild, the
connector hinted-close delta path, and the drop-rollback path.

runtime-next: bound gRPC status messages so errors survive the wire

A task error whose formatted chain was very large (e.g. the causal-hint
resolution timeout, which dumped one line per unresolved producer) could
not survive leader -> shard propagation: gRPC status text rides in an
HTTP/2 trailer, and an oversized trailer trips h2's `too_many_continuations`
guard, which aborts the connection and replaces the real status text with
an opaque transport error. The true cause was invisible in the surfaced
task error.

Bound every status message we emit to MAX_STATUS_MESSAGE_LEN so it fits
within a single HTTP/2 frame and never needs a CONTINUATION frame.
Truncation is from the tail, preserving the human-meaningful prefix the
anyhow format leads with. This covers both the errors we format ourselves
(`anyhow_to_status` and the leader materialize/derive handlers) and statuses
we merely pass through -- one round-tripped from a peer or produced by a
connector -- so a misbehaving connector emitting a huge message can't
produce a status that's dropped in transit. Pass-through statuses are
rebuilt preserving their code, details, and metadata.

shuffle: bound causal-hint-timeout error detail

On a causal-hint resolution timeout, `on_tick` appended a line per
unresolved producer with no cap, producing a multi-thousand-line error
when many hints were stuck (a real incident stalled on ~1400 hints across
~540 journals). Besides being unreadable, the string was truncated by the
log pipeline and too large to cross gRPC.

Factor the detail out into a pure `Frontier::describe_unresolved`, which
renders at most DESCRIBE_UNRESOLVED_MAX_LINES producer lines and elides the
rest as "… and N more unresolved hint(s)" (N derived from unresolved_hints,
no second walk). The error is now bounded at the source regardless of hint
count, keeping it readable in the logs.

Part of estuary/flow#3177.

control-plane: guarded, auto-expiring temporary support access to restricted tenants (#3115)

* supabase: guarded, auto-expiring temporary support access to restricted tenants

Restricted tenants are deliberately not attached to estuary_support/, so
support cannot reach them by default. This adds an internal.support_access
tracking table plus SECURITY DEFINER functions to grant, revoke, and expire
temporary support access to a single tenant.

Operators receive EXECUTE on the functions (granted out of band by the
departmental-roles tooling) and never write public.role_grants directly, so
they cannot escalate their own access. The grant function only attaches
estuary_support/ to a named, existing tenant and logs who granted it, why,
and when it expires.

Expiry is enforced by pg_cron on the Supabase database, registered out of
band since pg_cron is absent from the sqlx test cluster. The sweeper only
removes grants that have a support_access tracking row, so the permanent
estuary_support/ grants normal tenants receive are never affected.

Adds pgTAP coverage in supabase/tests/support_access.test.sql.

Implements ADR estuary/security#746.

* supabase: only delete support grants owned by a tracking row

The temporary-access functions matched role_grants rows solely on
(subject_role, object_role), so they could not tell a temporary grant
from the permanent estuary_support/ grant every unrestricted tenant
carries:

- grant_support_access() on an unrestricted tenant hit the unique
  conflict, did nothing, but still inserted a tracking row -- arming
  expire_support_access() to delete the permanent grant later.
- revoke_support_access() deleted unconditionally, wiping a permanent
  grant with no audit trace.
- Overlapping windows (a grant extended before it lapsed) share one
  role_grants row; expiring the earlier window detached the tenant
  while the later window was still open.

A role_grants row is now deleted only while an unrevoked
support_access row owns it: grant refuses unrestricted tenants unless
extending an active window, revoke requires an active tracking row,
and the sweeper skips tenants that still have an open window (and
counts only rows actually detached).

Also switch the functions to the repo-wide `set search_path to ''`
SECURITY DEFINER convention, and extend the pgTAP tests to cover the
unrestricted-tenant and overlapping-window cases with exact error
message assertions.

* supabase: move grant expiry onto role_grants/user_grants columns

Per PR review, expiration timestamps now live on the grant tables
themselves rather than only in the internal.support_access tracking
table: both role_grants and user_grants gain a nullable expires_at,
where NULL (every pre-existing row) means permanent. Enforcement is
unchanged from the sweeper design -- expired rows are DELETED on a
schedule -- so no Rust, RLS, authorization-function, or view changes
are needed; deletion propagates to every consumer by construction.

The columns make the safety guards structural rather than
ownership-tracked:

- grant_support_access() is one race-free upsert: a fresh grant inserts
  with an expiry, an extension takes the later expiry (greatest), and
  the conflict guard's WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL makes converting a
  permanent grant impossible (greatest(NULL, x) = x, so the guard is
  load-bearing). The audit row records the effective expiry.
- revoke_support_access() deletes only rows with a non-NULL expires_at,
  so it cannot detach an unrestricted tenant's permanent grant. It
  deletes immediately: with no read-side expiry filters, a
  lapsed-but-unswept row is still live access.
- expire_support_access() sweeps both tables where expires_at has
  passed. Overlapping support windows share one row carrying the latest
  expiry, so nothing is removed while a window remains open, and
  permanent grants can never match.

expires_at gets SELECT-only column grants for PostgREST-facing roles:
readable (required for RETURNING-representation dashboard mutations,
pinned by the existing lives_ok tests) but writable only through the
SECURITY DEFINER functions. internal.support_access remains as the
append-only audit log.

Tests: pgTAP covers grant/extend/re-grant-over-lapsed/revoke semantics,
permanent-grant refusal, and the sweep across both tables, driven by
direct expires_at updates. Full pgTAP suite passes; the
control-plane-api suite passes serially against the migrated schema
with zero Rust changes, confirming forward compatibility of the added
columns.

* supabase: validate grant duration; audit revocation is explicit-only

Review feedback on the support-access functions:

- grant_support_access() rejects a NULL or non-positive duration. A NULL
  duration computed a NULL expires_at, a permanent-looking grant; the
  audit insert's NOT NULL constraint would abort the transaction anyway,
  but only with a confusing error.
- expire_support_access() no longer stamps audit rows revoked. Audit
  rows carry per-request expiries that an extension deliberately does
  not move, so the sweep could mark a subsumed window as revoked by
  enforcement while the tenant's access was still live, and the
  sentinel revoked_by string conflated enforcement with revocation.
  revoked_at/revoked_by now strictly record explicit revocation by a
  named person; a row with revoked_at NULL and a past expires_at lapsed
  on schedule.

* supabase: harden support-access extension and revoke paths

Fixes from a final review pass:

- revoke_support_access() stamps only windows still open (expires_at >
  now()). Without the filter, audit rows of long-lapsed windows (which
  stay revoked_at NULL by design) were mis-stamped as explicitly
  revoked by whoever next revoked that tenant, corrupting the
  access-review record.
- The extension upsert re-asserts capability = 'admin'. PostgREST RLS
  lets a tenant's own admins update role_grants.capability, so an
  extension could otherwise preserve an out-of-band downgrade while
  logging an admin-implying audit row.
- detail now stays with the request whose window is in force: a shorter
  no-op extension no longer re-attributes the standing window to the
  losing request.
- Partial indexes on role_grants/user_grants (expires_at) WHERE
  expires_at IS NOT NULL: the per-minute sweep matches almost no rows
  and otherwise sequential-scans both tables.
- The audit insert relies on the flowid domain default rather than
  calling internal.id_generator() explicitly, matching the table
  definition's comment.

Tests cover the lapsed-history revoke, the capability re-assert, and
the detail attribution.

private-networking: model private links as rows with controller-observed status

Private links were a flat `data_planes.private_links` JSON array edited by hand, with the controller's provisioning results in separate `*_link_endpoints` columns and no way to tie an endpoint back to the link that produced it or to see a link's status. Model each link as a row in `internal.data_plane_private_links` with a stable id, its desired `config`, and controller-owned observed `status`/`details`/`error`, so the API reads status rather than reverse-engineering it from opaque endpoint blobs.

* New `internal.data_plane_private_links` table, one row per link, unique on `(data_plane_id, provider, service_identity)` so a same-provider duplicate cannot collide on a Pulumi resource name and wedge the converge. A backfill, guarded by a pre-flight that aborts on legacy data the table cannot represent, seeds it from the existing column.
* A `generation` counter, bumped by a `before update of config, provider` trigger that also clears the observation columns, versions the desired config. The controller pins each link's `(id, generation)` when it reads desired state and records a converge's status only against a matching generation, so an edit racing a converge is never stamped with a status computed from the pre-edit config.
* The controller reads desired links from the table, sends each link's row id through the stack model, and records each link's status from est-dry-dock's `link_results` export (estuary/est-dry-dock#337) matched by id: `provisioned` with details, `failed` with its error. Outputs pre-dating the export parse as absent and write no statuses.
* There is no wake trigger: the poll loop's config diff picks up table edits, and an edit observed mid-converge queues a follow-up converge, since the generation guard makes the in-flight converge's status write skip the edited row.
* agent-api replaces the wholesale `updateDataPlanePrivateLinks` mutation with per-link `add`/`update`/`remove`, gated by `ModifyDataPlanePrivateNetworking`, and surfaces per-link status.

The legacy `private_links` and `*_link_endpoints` columns are left in place so a controller on the pre-deploy binary keeps working during the rolling deploy; link edits are paused for the deploy window so the frozen column and the table cannot disagree while both binaries run, and a follow-up drops the columns and recreates `data_planes_overview`.

shuffle: log canonical journal name in slice read events

process_read_result logged the journal from read.fragment().journal,
which is empty for any read that has not yet observed a fragment-bearing
ReadResponse. A caught-up tailing read whose blocking metadata fetch
closes with EOF before any response never populates that fragment, so
its transient-EOF WARN (and every other event in this function) logged
an empty journal field. Use read_state.journal, the canonical journal
name that is always populated, matching the stall-track events.

runtime: persist the max-key fail-safe sentinel at adoption

The V1 runtime can commit checkpoint progress for a binding without ever
observing one of its keys (e.g. via ACK-only journal reads), in which case
no MK-v2: max-key is persisted. On the next recovery the binding is active
in the checkpoint without a persisted max-key, and recovery adopts a [0xff]
fail-safe sentinel in memory only. Because no packed key compares greater
than [0xff], the binding's max-key never ratchets again and is never
persisted -- permanently.

This is end-to-end safe within V1 (the sentinel conservatively disables the
load-skip optimization), but it breaks V1 => V2 migration semantics: the V2
runtime interprets a missing max-key as "no keys were ever stored", which
enables the load-skip optimization for a binding that may hold extensive
stored data.

Close the loop by durably persisting the sentinel at the moment of adoption,
synchronized to the recovery log before any Load or Store of the session.
A missing MK-v2: key then once again means "no keys ever stored", matching
V2's native invariant, and migration requires no V2-side changes.

Recovery must also accept the persisted sentinel: it is intentionally not a
valid packed tuple (0xff is tuple::ESCAPE, above every type code), so it is
matched exactly and used verbatim rather than unpacked. Any other
unparseable value still fails as corruption. This same relaxation makes a
V2 => V1 rollback of a task carrying the sentinel recover cleanly.

local: make flow-plane-link robust to control-plane agent start-up

flow-plane-link is a Type=oneshot whose ExecStart curls the control-plane

failed, the oneshot failed, and systemctl start returned non-zero to the

--retry-connrefused re-issues while the agent isn't listening yet,
--retry covers transient 5xx during warm-up, bounded to 120s via
--retry-max-time. The agent binds its API port only once it can serve, so a
connection being accepted is a genuine readiness signal.

Verified: a fresh 'mise run local:stack' reaches the local-view publish with
plane-link succeeding first-try (NRestarts=0); the connection-refused retry
path is exercised in the unit's journal and the piped request body is sent
intact across retries.

flowctl: preview-next appends a final drain session

A materialization session halts after its final commit without running
its post-commit Acknowledge — that work belongs to the next session's
startup recovery. For a long-lived production task the next session
arrives promptly, but a preview is a terminal run: without a successor,
it exited reporting the final transaction committed while its effects
were absent from the endpoint.

Every materialization preview now appends one empty drain session, which
requests a graceful stop as soon as it opens: the leader completes its
startup tail — acknowledging the prior session's final transaction —
before honoring the stop. `--sessions 2` therefore means two sessions
whose work is fully applied on exit. A run aborted by timeout skips the
drain, like any other session.

control-plane-api: don't lock injected ops collections during publications (#3164)

* control-plane-api: don't lock injected ops collections during publications

Every publication injects ops.us-central1.v1/{logs,stats} into its build so
the runtime knows where to write telemetry. Those collections then landed in
the passthrough set that verify_unchanged_revisions locks with FOR UPDATE,
so every publication in the fleet took a row lock on the same two live_specs
rows, serializing all publishes globally (estuary/sre#54).

The publication does not modify these collections and has no correctness
dependency on their last_pub_id, so skip locking and revision-checking them.
They remain injected into the build, and a publication which actually drafts
an ops collection is still locked and validated through the normal
drafted-spec path.

Adds a regression test which bumps the ops collections' last_pub_id between
an unrelated publication's build and commit, and asserts the commit still
succeeds; without this change it fails with a BuildIdLockFailure on the two
ops rows.

* control-plane-api: still revision-check ops collections read by drafted specs

Review follow-ups to the previous commit:

The lock-skip of injected ops collections was by name alone, so it also
dropped the revision check when a drafted spec genuinely reads an ops
collection (as the L2 reporting derivations do). Now the skip only applies
to ops collections which are not a dependency of any drafted spec in the
build, so a genuinely-referenced ops collection is locked and revision
checked like any other dependency.

Also: document on get_ops_collection_names that injection and lock-skipping
must stay in agreement if it becomes data-plane-dependent, remove a dead
`if !expect_pub_id.is_zero() {}` leftover from an earlier refactor
(passthrough rows always have a non-zero pub id), and simplify the
regression test's draft construction and helper. The test now also covers
the referenced-ops case: a derivation reading ops.us-central1.v1/logs gets
a lock failure for exactly that collection when it changes mid-publication,
while the merely-injected stats collection remains unlocked.

runtime-next: force txn close at any usage ceiling, bypassing min duration

A saturated usage measure (e.g. combiner disk usage) means an open
transaction can make no further useful progress, so holding it open to
honor the minimum transaction duration just idles a doomed transaction.
Close it promptly instead.

The close policy is restructured around symmetric time/usage min/max
predicates so any ceiling breach forces close and waives all floors,
where previously a usage-max breach still respected the time floor.

Rewrite the evaluate() doc comment to explain the batching intent, and
extend test coverage (last-close floor, max-duration ceiling with usage
below floor, per-dimension usage ceilings, wake_after).

gazette: terminate a bounded read when a fragment hole spans end_offset

A fragment hole can fast-forward `req.offset` to or past a bounded read's
`end_offset`. The `req.offset == end_offset` termination check misses that
case and the read wedges past the range it was asked for. Use `>=`, and
additionally terminate right after the metadata refresh once the resolved
offset covers the requested range — yielding the metadata first so the
caller observes the resolved offset.

Prerequisite for shuffle's bounded historical replay reads.

service-kit: accept a runtime Level in event!

`tracing::event!` bakes its level into a `static` callsite and so requires
a constant. Fan a runtime `$level` out to one constant-level `tracing::event!`
per level and select at runtime; only the taken branch renders, and a literal
level still folds to a single callsite. This lets a call site log more quietly
on a first attempt and louder on retry.

Adds the `__event_at_level!` plumbing macro and a test exercising a runtime
level.

shuffle: factor read-failure classification and batch parsing out of the read loop

Extract two pure helpers from `SliceActor::process_read_result` into `read.rs`:

  - `classify_read_failure` maps a `RetryError` into JournalRemoved (benign),
    Transient (retry-able, with attempt count), or Terminal (fail).
  - `parse_lines_batch` transcodes a `LinesBatch` to archived documents, puts
    back any unparsed remainder, extracts and validates per-document metadata,
    and pairs the head document with its metadata.

A forthcoming historical replay read will share the same parsing and error
handling. Behavior is preserved apart from log-level tuning enabled by the
runtime-level `event!`: a benign journal removal now logs at DEBUG, and a
transient read error is quiet (TRACE) on its first attempt and WARN thereafter.

shuffle: replay gapped producers on restart

On restart a `(binding, journal)` read resumes at the furthest position its
checkpoint justifies: the maximum offset magnitude `M` across producer entries.
An uncommitted producer span whose begin offset `F` falls before `M` is
*gapped* — the main read skips `[F, M)` and would silently drop the span's
documents. Recover these spans instead of dropping them:

  - `resolve_checkpoint` marks a gapped producer with the in-memory sentinel
    `max_continue == last_commit` (non-zero) (`ProducerState::is_gapped`),
    pinning its `offset` at `F`. The sentinel cannot arise organically:
    `uuid::sequence` raises `max_continue` only to a CONTINUE clock strictly
    above `last_commit`, and advances `last_commit` only while `max_continue`
    is zero — so a live `max_continue` is always zero or strictly above
    `last_commit`, never equal. `sequence_producer` (the pure, single
    sequencing path for gapped and non-gapped producers alike) reports the
    first newer CONTINUE or ACK as a replay trigger.

  - On a trigger the actor reconstructs the open span, then opens a single
    bounded historical read of `[F, trigger.begin)` (the new `Replay`,
    `slice/replay.rs`). Its sequenced documents append before everything in the
    heap — including the trigger — then the trigger is re-presented to the
    normal path. A replay head-of-line-blocks the Slice until it completes.

Checkpoint durability underpins this: `build_flush_frontier` floors every
read-derived `last_commit` at `OBSERVED_COMMIT_FLOOR` (raw 1), so recovery can
tell a real span begun at journal offset zero from a hint-only placeholder
`{0, 0}`. `ProducerFrontier::reduce` breaks an equal-magnitude offset tie in
favor of the uncommitted (non-negative) begin, and `resolve_hints` flips a
hint-resolved span's offset to the cut floor `-M` so a settled span recovers
un-gapped and never re-replays. `max_continue` itself is never persisted.

Adds replay start/stop metrics and a `Drop` for `SliceActor` that balances the
started/stopped counters on teardown. Covers the feature with new fixture
scenarios (ACK- and CONTINUE-triggered replays, cross-journal blocking, the
hint-elevated offset flip, and the gapped-OUTSIDE protocol violation), a unit
test covering a producer whose next-transaction span opens at a clock adjacent
to its prior commit, and extends the fuzz harness with open-span actions
(ContinueOnly/CommitOpen), production hint-fidelity in its projection, and
deterministic regression cases. Removes the superseded fuzz-testing-reqs doc.

runtime-next: widen frontier-prune horizons (48h / 8GiB)

Raise FRONTIER_PRUNE_CLOCK_HORIZON from 2h to 48h and
FRONTIER_PRUNE_BYTE_HORIZON from 2GiB back to 8GiB, so recovery retains
stale committed-frontier producers far longer before pruning them.

Pruning an FC: producer forgets its uncommitted span; retaining it lets
that span be recovered rather than dropped. What changed is the cost of
retention. Restarts used to be conservative: the main read resumed at the
*earliest* producer offset, so a single retained laggard at offset F
dragged the entire (binding, journal) read back to F and forced a full
re-read of every producer from there -- the operational cost the 2GiB
horizon was tuned to bound.

Restarts are now optimistic (see "shuffle: replay gapped producers on
restart"): the read resumes at the *maximum* offset magnitude M, and a
laggard whose span begins at F < M is replayed by a single bounded
historical read of just [F, trigger.begin), only if that producer
resumes. The cost of keeping a laggard is now a localized, per-producer
replay instead of pulling the whole read backwards -- so retaining more
is preferable to silently dropping the span, and the horizons can be
conservative. 8GiB also restores the pre-0846abb2bb8 byte horizon, which
had been lowered only to prune sooner before replay existed.

Adjusts the prune-policy test to bracket the new horizons; outcome is
unchanged.

Documentation for https://github.com/estuary/connectors/pull/4835.

dekaf: only read back when a fetch offset lands inside a document

The mid-document readback (#3150) started every new journal read up to
OFFSET_READBACK (64MB) before the fetch offset, re-reading and discarding
that span to locate the containing document. Consumers which frequently
start new reads pay that cost on nearly every fetch, multiplying Dekaf's
broker-side read volume by orders of magnitude and stalling delivery
behind suppression scans.

Reads now begin exactly at the offset being served and probe whether it
is a document boundary: the stream's first document either carries a
valid UUID at the collection's UUID pointer (boundary; no readback), or
it proves a mid-document landing (parse error, or parsed JSON without a
valid UUID) and the read restarts with readback. Stream rebuilds on
token refresh also skip readback, since a read's offset is a served
document's end once any document has been served.

Readback restarts are counted by a new dekaf_readback_restarts metric,
and e2e tests assert that mid-document fetches record a restart while
boundary fetches record none.

dekaf: probe one byte before the fetch offset

The parser treats a document's trailing newline as inter-document
whitespace and skips it silently, so a probe which begins exactly at the
fetch offset mis-verifies fetches addressing a document's final byte:
the stream starts at the separator and cleanly parses the *next*
document, dropping the one the offset addresses. That final byte is
precisely the Kafka offset assigned to the document, and the e2e
mid-document test caught the regression deterministically.

An offset is a document boundary exactly when the byte before it is a
separator newline, so the probe now starts one byte earlier: boundary
probes skip that newline and verify on the following document, while a
fetch at a document's final byte reads its last content byte as an
unparseable suffix and correctly restarts with readback.

dekaf: detect document boundaries by reading the preceding byte

Replaces the parse-based probe with a direct check, per review: collection
journals are newline-delimited JSON — documents are written compactly with
exactly one terminating newline, and JSON forbids unescaped control
characters — so a raw newline byte occurs in journal content only as a
document terminator. An offset is therefore a boundary exactly when the
preceding byte is a newline, which a single-byte non-blocking point read
determines before the stream is opened, replacing the probe state machine
in next_batch (which returns to its pre-probe shape).

If that byte is unavailable — offset zero, at or beyond the write head,
expired from the journal, or the journal suspended or deleted — no
containing document can be served regardless, and the read begins at the
fetch offset.

The metric is renamed dekaf_readback_restarts -> dekaf_readback_reads,
since a readback now starts the stream rather than restarting it.

mise: dev-VM zone configurability (create fallback, zone-agnostic SSH, vm:move-gcp) (#3208)

* mise: make dev-VM zones configurable and add vm:move-gcp

Dev VMs restart in a single pinned zone, so a ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED
error in that zone strands the VM until GCP frees capacity there. Three
changes:

- vm:create-gcp accepts an ordered comma-separated --zone list and falls
  through to the next zone on capacity errors (only), defaulting to
  us-central1-b,us-central1-c,us-east5-a,us-east4-a.
- The generated SSH ProxyCommand discovers the instance's zone at connect
  time instead of hardcoding it, so configs survive zone moves.
- New vm:move-gcp relocates an existing VM to a new zone by snapshotting
  its boot disk (machine images don't support Hyperdisk, which is all C4
  machines can attach) and recreating the instance around the restored
  disk. The original is renamed, not deleted, until the replacement passes
  an SSH check, so a failed move can never lose the VM.

Shared helpers live in mise/tasks/vm/gcp-lib.sh, sourced by both tasks.

* mise: forget stale SSH host keys before connecting to dev VMs

Found by a live move test: cloud-init regenerates host keys whenever the
instance-id changes, which happens on every zone move and when recreating
a VM under a reused name. The generated configs use strict host-key
checking against ~/.ssh/gcp-vms/hosts, so the stale entry made every
post-move connection fail until the 36-attempt wait loop expired (the
move's safety design held: nothing was deleted, and the printed recovery
manifest was sufficient to finish the move by hand).

Drop the instance's known-hosts entry before the first connection in both
create-gcp and move-gcp; StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new then records
the fresh key over the Google-authenticated IAP tunnel.

* mise: review fixes for dev-VM zone tasks

- Trim whitespace and skip empty items when splitting --zone lists, so
  "a, b" style input works in both tasks. move-gcp quoted the raw item
  and would silently drop " b" with a misleading "not offered" warning.
- move-gcp now mirrors the source boot disk's type instead of assuming
  hyperdisk-balanced, so hand-built VMs with Persistent Disk boot
  volumes move without a mid-flight attach failure.

runtime-next: converge startup reconciliation via rescan Persists

Rework leader startup reconciliation from a one-shot cleanup Persist into
an iterative convergence loop. `reconcile_loop` repeatedly reconciles the
scanned RocksDB `Baseline` against its authoritative checkpoints, applying
each self-clearing step as a `rescan` Persist and re-reading the freshly
written durable state before the next iteration. Session startup state is
then a projection of the actually-scanned durable state rather than of an
in-memory reconstruction, so the leader can never diverge from disk.

The reconcile policy is factored into a pure, IO-free `reconcile` function
(one per derive/materialize) expressed as an ordered sequence of triggered,
self-clearing steps: convert a V1-written legacy checkpoint, drop V1
rollback, fold a hinted commit the connector confirms, and adopt a
connector checkpoint that committed ahead. `frontier_mapping::adopt_checkpoint`
builds the Persist that adopts a checkpoint wholesale, and
`COMMITTED_CLOSE_FLOOR` seeds the committed close when an adopted checkpoint
carries no embedded Clock.

Shard actors gain `rescan` handling: a rescan Persist re-scans the DB and
replies with a fresh `Recover` (rather than a `Persisted` echo) so the
leader observes reconciled on-disk state.

const so the floor Clock is a constant.

Fix a crash-loop in the remote-authoritative connector case
===========================================================

The old materialize reconciliation applied the hinted-commit fold — the
case where the connector's checkpoint confirms a recovered hinted
transaction did in fact commit at the endpoint — purely in memory. It
advanced `committed_close` and reduced the committed Frontier for the
session, but emitted no Persist (it set neither `committed_frontier_rebuilt`
nor a cleanup Persist), so RocksDB's `committed_close` stayed at its
pre-fold value.

That left durable state inconsistent with the endpoint. A session could:

  1. start up and fold a hinted commit the endpoint had confirmed (in
     memory only — `committed_close` on disk unchanged),
  2. run a transaction that wrote the *next* hint via StartCommit (bumping
     the on-disk `hinted_close`), then
  3. crash before that transaction committed at the endpoint.

The subsequent recovery then saw a stale on-disk `committed_close`, a newer
`hinted_close`, and an endpoint clock equal to the folded value — which
matched neither — so `reconcile_recovered` hit its mismatch `bail!`. Because
the crash never changed durable state, every recovery re-derived the same
mismatch and the shard crash-looped.

Routing the fold through `reconcile_loop` as a `rescan` Persist makes the
advance durable: `committed_close` moves on disk during the fold recovery,
so a later next-hint crash recovers with the endpoint clock matching the
persisted `committed_close` (the in-sync branch) and never bails. Covered
by the `reconcile_fold_then_next_hint_matches_committed_close` regression
test.

control-plane-api: surface per-store health diagnostics in storage-mapping mutations (#3181)

createStorageMapping and updateStorageMapping ran per-store fragment-store health checks but collapsed any failure into a generic "Storage health checks failed" error, discarding the per-store diagnostics that run_all_health_checks had already collected. Building on the gazette change that surfaces the store's real error string, thread those diagnostics into both mutation errors: a new describe_health_failures helper renders each failing check as its store URL, data-plane name, and the store's own error. testConnectionHealth already returned full per-store results and is unchanged.

async-process: handle reaping-task failure without panicking

Child::wait() previously unwrap()'d the JoinHandle of the spawn_blocking
task which reaps the child, panicking if that task was cancelled by
runtime teardown (a routine path, e.g. a cancelled shard context) or
panicked. Worse, an aborted reaping task reports is_finished() == true,
so Drop concluded the child had already exited and skipped the SIGKILL,
leaking a live process.

Replace the Result-based status with an explicit state machine:
Reaping (task blocked in wait()), Reaped (exit status collected), and
Abandoned (task terminated without reaping). wait() now surfaces an
io::Error instead of panicking, and Drop dispatches on the state:
Reaped is left alone (pid may be recycled), Reaping is SIGKILLed (the
blocked task reaps), and Abandoned is SIGKILLed *and* reaped, since
nobody else will and it would otherwise linger as a zombie.

Add regression tests driving real child processes through both
JoinError variants, covering wait() and the drop-without-wait path
relied on by container guards.

proto: add backfill truncation messages

Backfill truncation lets a capture re-backfill a binding and mark the
previously-captured data as stale. It needs new protocol surface:
capture BackfillBegin / BackfillComplete responses, materialize Flush
backfill notifications, runtime Recover.active_backfills and a Persist
active-backfill change, and shuffle Frontier latest_backfill_{begin,
complete} clocks keyed by binding index.

labels: add truncated-at journal label

A reader must skip the stale pre-backfill prefix of a journal once its
binding is re-backfilled. Record the boundary as an
`estuary.dev/truncated-at` label: a fixed-width hex Gazette clock that
sorts lexically by value and only ever advances. dekaf honors it by
raising its effective not_before to the max truncated-at of its journals.

doc: truncate the combiner at per-binding backfill boundaries

A materialization that loads a stale row — one published before its
binding's backfill boundary — must not reduce it into the fresh, current
document for the same key, or the superseded value would leak forward.

Expose an explicit Accumulator::truncate(binding): the live MemTable
drops the binding's pre-boundary sources and flags its Loaded fronts
stale, while already-spilled segments are fenced by a per-binding ordinal
cutoff. Staleness is a single Meta flag bit, keeping HeapEntry at 32
bytes and the spill entry header at 24.

shuffle: propagate backfill clocks through the frontier

Fold the begin/complete clocks of backfill markers into the checkpoint
frontier, keyed by binding index. The markers ride the bodies of
immediately-committed ACK documents, so they never participate in
causal-hint sequencing; their clocks are instead max-reduced per binding
across a checkpoint delta and surface on a resolved NextCheckpoint.

publisher: carry backfill markers on ACK documents and apply truncated-at labels

A backfill marker rides the body of a transaction's ACK documents,
broadcast to every partition journal of the binding under a single
shared clock, so even a constrained reader observes it. Un-upgraded
readers skip ACKs, so the marker is invisible to them by construction
and commits atomically with the connector checkpoint. Also apply the
`estuary.dev/truncated-at` label to a binding's journals.

runtime-next: persist backfill-truncation state in RocksDB

Backfill state must survive transaction rotation and leader restart.
Add key families, split by task type: `AB:` holds a capture's
in-progress active backfills (the clocks that drive the truncated-at
journal label), while `BB:`/`BC:` (and hinted `HB:`/`HC:`) hold a
materialization's cumulative begin/complete boundary keyed by state_key.

runtime-next: emit backfill markers from captures

A capture connector may signal BackfillBegin / BackfillComplete for a
binding. Each signal must stand alone in its connector checkpoint, so
isolate it in its own transaction, publish the marker on that
transaction's ACK documents — the begin's assigned clock is the
authoritative truncated_at — and stage the active-backfill change
atomically with the connector checkpoint.

runtime-next: apply backfill truncation in materializations

Carry the per-binding truncation boundary from the frontier into the
shard. The scan drops source documents older than the boundary, and a
loaded row older than it is classified prior-generation so the combiner
discards it instead of reducing stale state forward — its
current-generation sibling is then stored as an update. The leader
broadcasts each begin/complete notification to every shard's connector.

data-plane-controller: add GitHub App git auth to replace SSH machine user (#3243)

* data-plane-controller: add GitHub App git auth to replace SSH machine user

DPC clones estuary/est-dry-dock at runtime as the estuary-dpc machine user
via an SSH key. Org SAML SSO enforcement will lock out that non-identity
account, so move git auth to a GitHub App, whose identities are exempt.

Auth stays ambient in entrypoint.sh, as it is today, so the worker code does
not change. Because App installation tokens expire hourly, a static
credential is not enough; a git credential helper supplies fresh tokens on
demand. A new `git-credential` subcommand signs an RS256 App JWT, exchanges
it for an installation token, caches it to disk until shortly before expiry,
and returns it to git over the credential protocol. The token never touches a
command line or on-disk git config, so it cannot leak into command logs.

entrypoint.sh gains a DPC_GIT_AUTH_MODE switch (default ssh); in github-app
mode it rewrites the remote to HTTPS and registers the helper. The service
deploy workflow gains the App key secret and the App/Installation IDs. Default
ssh means merging and deploying change nothing until the mode is flipped;
flipping back to ssh is the rollback.

  stdout carries only username=/password= and the clone still succeeds.

vm: fix Lima development VMs on Linux hosts (#3267)

* vm: fix Lima development VMs on Linux hosts

Three independent defects made `vm:create-lima` unusable on a Linux host,
and left `vm:create-post` unable to run a second time.

Drop the `user-v2` network on Linux. It *replaces* Lima's built-in NIC
rather than adding to it, so QEMU is given a single `-netdev socket,fd=N`
carrying all guest traffic, served by Lima's embedded gvisor-tap-vsock over
a unix stream. Under any sustained transfer (first-boot `apt`, the repo
clone, later `cargo fetch`) that stream desynchronizes and QEMU aborts:

    qemu-system-x86_64: ../net/net.c:2172:
      net_fill_rstate: Assertion `size == 0' failed.

killing the VM mid-provision. The defect is unfixed upstream and appears
unreported, since the QEMU stream protocol is used almost exclusively by
Lima on Linux. Removing the entry costs only VM-to-VM connectivity, which
the vz branch already forgoes on macOS, so no developer loses a capability
another one has. Verified from scratch: creation, the 3.2GB clone, the full
local stack (14 units, 0 failed), and a 624MB download at 22MB/s run
concurrently with a cargo build.

Make the ssh_config edit converge. The guard was `grep -q lima`, which
matches that string anywhere in the file, and the block only ever prepended
when absent. Once a copy ended up below a `Host` stanza (which happens as
soon as anything is added above it) ssh scoped the Include to that one
host, `ssh lima-<name>` failed to resolve, and the guard passed forever so
this never repaired it. Strip any copy we previously wrote, wherever it
sits, then prepend.

Since that rewrite is now unconditional, it also writes only when the
content actually changes, and writes through the existing file instead of
moving one in over it. Otherwise every invocation would relabel the config
under SELinux (mktemp yields `user_tmp_t`, policy wants `ssh_home_t`),
replace a dotfile-managed symlink with a regular file, reset its mode, and
make concurrent runs last-writer-wins.

Recycle the user manager after `usermod`. `usermod` only edits /etc/group,
and running processes keep the groups they started with. `systemd --user`
is already up, so every unit it later spawns inherits the old set: the
stack's units fail with EACCES on the docker socket while an interactive
shell looks correct, and the first `local:stack` on a new VM always fails.
Restarting the manager from the system manager re-resolves credentials in a
fresh process. It is conditional on a group actually being absent, so
re-running create-post on a healthy VM does not tear down a running stack
along with the manager, and it checks both groups added above it rather
than docker alone. `loginctl terminate-user` also recycles the manager, but
destroys the session it arrives on along with /run/user/$UID, leaving
logind wedged and `systemctl --user` unusable.

Guard the swapfile creation. On an already-provisioned VM the swapfile is
active, so `fallocate` fails with ETXTBSY, which aborts the task under
`set -e` and stops every later step from running. Re-running create-post is
the documented way to diagnose a bad first boot, so it has to survive a
second run.

Both new guards avoid piping into `grep -q`, which exits on its first match
and can leave the writer killed by SIGPIPE; under `set -o pipefail` that
non-zero status inverts the very condition being tested.

* local: clear a stale container name before starting the bigtable emulator

`ExecStart` runs `docker run --rm --name flow-bigtable-%i`, and `--rm` cleans up
on a normal exit. It does not help when the unit loses track of a container that
is still running, which happens whenever `systemd --user` is recycled: the
container belongs to dockerd, survives, and keeps the name. `docker run` then
fails with

    Conflict. The container name "/flow-bigtable-%i" is already in use

and since `Restart=on-failure` retries every 5s forever, the unit never recovers.
Observed in the wild at a restart counter of 1198, roughly three hours of looping,
while the emulator itself was up and serving the whole time, so the stack looked
broken in `systemctl` but worked.

Add the `ExecStartPre=-docker rm -f` that flow-dekaf-kafka@.service already
carries for exactly this reason.

publisher: discard unauthorized recovered ACK intents

`write_intents` now tolerates `PermissionDenied` on its ephemeral path,
alongside the `NotFound` it already discards. Without this, a task holding a
recovered intent for a journal it's no longer authorized to crash-loops
forever: the session fails, recovers the identical intent, and fails again.

Nothing clears an intent but writing it, and the task cannot heal itself —
updating it to no longer publish to the journal is precisely what stranded the
intent. Fail-open is the only terminating choice. The tolerance is safe because
only recovered intents reach the ephemeral path: a live transaction's intents
are keyed on journals it just wrote, so they always match a binding and
continue to fail strictly.

Observed after a data-plane migration, where the recovered intent named the
prior plane's ops stats journal, but the same failure follows any revoked grant
on a collection the task published to under an earlier specification.

Runtime-v1's narrower accommodation in `go/runtime/authorizer.go` is left as-is:
it cannot express the "matches no current binding" predicate from the authorizer
layer, and v1 is being retired.

runtime-next: remove hardcoded materialization ser_policy fallback

The runtime has sniffed endpoint config bytes for well-known connector
image names and applied a hardcoded truncation policy on match, because
those connectors couldn't yet negotiate one. Serialization policies are
now negotiated via the connector protocol: connectors return ser_policy
in their Validated response and it's baked into the built binding spec,
which build_binding already prefers.

All six formerly-hardcoded connectors now return ser_policy (redshift,
azure-fabric-warehouse, and sqlite as of estuary/connectors#4787), and
the 20-day periodic touch publication cycle refreshes every enabled
task's built spec, so the fallback is dead weight. Bindings without a
policy now get SerPolicy::noop().

This resolves the TODO(johnny) hack comment and the TODO(whb) removal
condition. The V1 runtime keeps its copy of the hack; it's deprecated
and not worth touching.

go/runtime: bind task terms to ShardSpec bytes, not pointer identity

A task term was bound to the decoded *pf.ShardSpec pointer, and
signalOnSpecUpdate ended the term whenever that pointer stopped matching
the KeySpace's currently-decoded value. But any re-decode of the key
re-mints the pointer, so a byte-identical re-PUT of the ShardSpec -- as
the control plane's do_activate restart path can emit -- cancelled the
terms of every live, healthy shard of the task.

Bind each term to the raw etcd value bytes instead. newTaskTerm captures
the decoded spec and its Raw.Value coherently from the same KeyValue
under a single read lock, and signalOnSpecUpdate compares bytes.Equal
against the current value on each wakeup, so only a real value change or
a deletion ends the term. The taskSpec-reuse optimization compares bytes
as well, so a no-op re-PUT no longer needlessly re-opens the build DB.

Part of #3247.

go/runtime: term cancellation during Join-wait gracefully restarts the session

The pre-Opened Join-wait phase of a runtime-v2 session treated a
term-context cancellation as fatal: WaitForRevision's error failed the
shard. But the post-Opened steady state handles the identical
cancellation gracefully (Stop/Stopped drain, return nil, in-process
restart). This asymmetry contradicted the term contract in task.go -- "a
cancellation of the term's Context doesn't invalidate the shard" -- and,
together with the byte-identical re-PUTs of the prior commit, drove
multi-shard tasks into a self-sustaining restart loop.

Treat a Join-wait term cancellation as a graceful in-process restart:
when WaitForRevision errors but the shard context is still live, the
cancellation came from a spec update, so log at INFO and return nil. The
framework then loops back through RestoreCheckpoint with a fresh term.
This is safe pre-consensus because the Rust sidecar's session loop is
parked cleanly awaiting a Join and can immediately re-Join on the same
long-lived stream; the post-consensus window is already covered by the
steady-state drain. Applied identically to materialize and derive.

Part of #3247.

Extend `PrefixFilter` with `in` and add storage mapping query as a consumer (#3242)

shuffle: red regression tests for open-phase deadlock (#3245)

Add crate-level regression tests reproducing the multi-shard shuffle
open deadlock described in issue #3245: when a peer sidecar is briefly
unreachable during the Session -> Slice -> Log open fan-out, the peer's
error is trapped by `join_all` while sibling in-process opens park
forever on a Log rendezvous that can never complete.

Three tests spin two in-process `Service` instances with distinct
`peer_endpoint`s (one serving real loopback tonic):

- open_errors_when_peer_dial_refused: a peer endpoint that refuses
  connections instantly must promptly error `open`.
- open_errors_when_reachable_peer_rejects: a reachable peer whose Slice
  open is rejected must error `open` and drain both `log_joins` maps.
- retry_after_abort_reuses_directory: a partial rendezvous that aborts
  must not poison a retry reusing the same shard directories.

Each is wrapped in a 30s `tokio::time::timeout` hang guard. Against the
unfixed code all three fail by exhausting that timeout (they hang);
the structural fix follows.

shuffle: fix open-phase deadlock via EOF-cascade teardown (#3245)

The Session->Slice->Log open fan-outs used `futures::future::join_all`,
which does not short-circuit on Err: a peer's connection-refused error
resolved but was trapped while sibling in-process opens parked forever
on the Log rendezvous (which only completes once ALL Slices connect).
The parked handlers are detached tasks not polling their request
streams, so teardown was never observed, and partial rendezvous state
in the process-global `Service::log_joins` map poisoned in-tenure
retries with "received duplicate Slice connection". A multi-shard V2
task then wedged forever at startup whenever a peer sidecar was briefly
unreachable.

Make the opening phase participate in the same request-stream-EOF
teardown cascade the running phase already uses:

- Session/Slice handlers replace `join_all` with `try_join_all`, raced
  via `tokio::select!` against the handler's own request stream. The
  first downstream open error short-circuits and drops the sibling open
  futures, cascading EOF teardown downward; an EOF/error/message on the
  request stream during opening (all illegal before `Opened`) aborts the
  same way (`opening_aborted`).

- The Log rendezvous is abort-safe: a non-completing invocation no
  longer returns `Ok` immediately after registering. It parks on a
  per-slot `oneshot` completion signal vs `response_tx.closed()`, and on
  `closed()` reaps only its own slot under the `log_joins` mutex
  (dropping the entry when its last live slot is removed), resolving the
  race with a concurrent completer.

- `LogJoin` is keyed by `(directory, session_id, log_shard_index)`;
  `session_id` makes retries collision-free by construction, so the
  abort cleanup only prevents leaks. The duplicate-slice-connection
  check remains as an intra-session protocol assertion.

Deliberately no deadlines and no stall watchdog anywhere: every
transient failure now errors and self-heals via try_join_all plus the
Go retry loop, and the rare residual (likely persistent) wedge classes
are easier to debug as a stable wedge than a flapping teardown/retry
loop. The crate README "Shutdown" section documents this.

The three regression tests from the prior commit now pass in ~0.07s.

runtime-next: hoist actor-loop timers and skip zero-duration sleeps

Every `wake_after` actor loop rebuilt `tokio::time::sleep(wake_after)` on
each iteration as its lowest-priority `select!` arm. That registered a
timer into — and on drop removed it from — the tokio runtime's single
global timer wheel, taking that mutex twice per iteration for every actor
in the process.

Worse, `wake_after` is frequently ZERO, meaning the loop's FSMs have
synchronous work already queued and want to be stepped again immediately.
`sleep(ZERO)` is not free: `TimeSource::deadline_to_tick` rounds every
deadline up to the end of the current millisecond, so the loop parked for
up to 1ms per step — capping input-free FSM sequences (rotate, drain,
persist, write-intents) near 1000 steps per second. Inserting at the
earliest possible tick also unparked the time driver on nearly every call.

Replace the arm with `sleep_unless_zero`, which returns immediately on
ZERO and otherwise resets a `Sleep` hoisted out of the caller's loop.
Resetting a live timer to a later deadline lands on
`TimerEntry::extend_expiration`'s lock-free CAS, so only the first
non-zero iteration of a loop takes the wheel mutex.

No `yield_now` on the ZERO path: the mpsc arms polled by every iteration
consume tokio's cooperative budget, which forces a yield within ~128
iterations. Bursting between those yields is wanted for cache and branch
behavior.

Non-zero durations are deliberately not collapsed, even below the 1ms
tick. They are deadline-driven — `leader::close_policy` reports the time
remaining until its nearest threshold, which shrinks to microseconds as
that threshold nears — so returning early would spin the loop
re-evaluating a deadline that has not passed.

runtime-next: hoist the IAM token-restart timers out of actor loops

`select!` rebuilds every arm's future on each iteration, so the
`maybe_deadline(self.token_restart_at)` arm constructed a fresh
`sleep_until` per iteration — inserting into and removing from the tokio
runtime's single global timer wheel, taking that mutex twice, for a
deadline that `token_restart_deadline` places 5 to 30 minutes ahead of
credential expiry (so, hours away). The arm is ungated and the deadline is
Some for any task with injected IAM credentials.

Both loops that carry it are hot: the capture actor reaches its `select!`
once per FSM step, and the materialize actor once per inbound connector
message (its high-volume arm). With the preceding commit's zero-duration
fix in place, this was the dominant remaining timer cost in those loops.

Hoist a stack-pinned `Sleep` out of each loop, as `shard/materialize`'s
`ticker` already does. Re-polling an already-registered timer is an atomic
waker registration plus one load, no lock. Absent injected credentials
there is no deadline, so arm it at `far_future()` rather than reintroducing
an Option — which also gives the fired arm a disarm: a `Sleep` that has
fired stays Ready forever and would otherwise win its arm on every
subsequent iteration, starving the lower-priority arms.

`token_restart_at` becomes write-once, consumed at loop entry, and both
copies of `maybe_deadline` lose their only caller and are deleted.
