shuffle: introduce the Frontier invariant and its ubiquitous language

Land the agreed vocabulary and invariant as prose, with no behavior change:

- The Frontier invariant is canonically stated on the `Frontier` type:
  a cumulative Frontier's entries describe one continuous read through
  each journal's cut floor M and account for every committing close and
  open span below it — which is what makes it sound to resume from. It
  is hint-state agnostic, reads inductively over reduction, and holds
  of deltas only relative to the base they reduce into.
- The shuffle README's Concepts section becomes the glossary: Span,
  Cut / cut floor, Open / Closed, Covered by, Accounts for, Gapped,
  Cumulative vs delta — plus terms to avoid (claim, subsume, vouch,
  settle, producer-completeness), each with its reason.
- Rename ReadState::pending/settled → unreported/reported, evicting
  "settle" from flush accounting so span closure owns the word "close".
- Sweep retired terms and old phrasing: "claim" is fully retired from
  domain prose, "uncommitted/pending span" becomes "open span", and the
  structural sorted/unique property is now the "Frontier ordering
  invariant" so the semantic invariant owns the bare name.
- `build_start_read`'s `take` note now says what makes dropping a
  journal's entries sound — the suspension contract, under which the
  journal's former content is gone and its resume offset is at-or-above
  the offset it suspended at — rather than asserting a start of zero.
- prune_committed_frontier documents itself as a deliberate, bounded
  relaxation of the invariant, with the clock/byte horizons framed as
  what bound the accepted double-processing risk.

runtime-v2: two-session idempotent recovery — park at the hinted frontier, then restart

An idempotent-recovery replay used to run as the first transaction of an
otherwise ordinary session: high-priority read cohorts finished their hinted
region and then tailed without bound into post-crash content that recovery
cannot consume. The pinned over-read grew with wall-clock, engaged global
disk back-pressure, and starved the low-priority cohort gating recovery
completion — timing out at CAUSAL_HINT_RESOLUTION_TIMEOUT with zero persisted
progress, then retrying against a larger backlog.

Split recovery and post-recovery work into two leader sessions. A session
which opens with unresolved hints does the replay and nothing else:

* Slice: each read counts its recovered unresolved hints and arms if the
  count is non-zero — which only a recovery session's reads can be. When the
  count reaches zero, at consumption of the resolving committing close (hence
  after any gap replay it triggered), the read parks: the in-hand batch tail
  and the ReadLines stream are dropped mid-batch. Its ReadState is retained,
  so the resolving flush delta still rides to the Session. Counting hints is
  what puts each producer's recovered `hinted_commit` on `slice::ProducerState`.

* Session: a recovery session issues StartRead only for (journal, binding)
  pairs carrying an unresolved hint, including skipping journals newly listed
  mid-recovery. `recovery_pending` becomes the sticky `recovery_session`:
  take_ready no longer clears it, so held-back progress is never promoted and
  the session quiesces after its one checkpoint.

* Leader: HeadIdle arms `stopping` as it closes an idempotent_replay
  transaction, so HeadStartCommit chains Persist(commit) → Head::Stop with no
  Rotate. The replayed transaction's Acknowledge and ACK-intent writes run as
  the next session's first act — the same path every crash restart uses.

The sticky pipeline and the leader exit are correct only together, hence one
commit.

Disk bound: the replay fits within the same shuffle disk limit the crashed
session ran under. Parking deletes the one unbounded disk term (post-hint
tailing); everything else the recovery session holds is either consumable
during replay or was equally held by the original session.

Parking loses nothing, by the Frontier invariant: the parked read's flush
delta reports a cut through the resolving close, and every close below it is
covered while any open span's `+begin` rides along, so the next session
resumes there whole.

The restart is correct but not yet cheap. The recovery checkpoint's producer
offsets sit at the cut floor the replay resumed from, so the next session
re-reads the whole hinted span before it makes new progress — a bounded,
one-off cost, and the subject of a follow-on commit. The
`resume_from_checkpoint` fixture records that re-read as its phase-3 byte
deltas.

Fixes #3246

shuffle: resolve cyclic hints from completed_clocks, not a reverse pass

Causal hints can be cyclic: journal A hints at a commit on B while B hints
at one on A, and the two arrive in distinct Progressed responses. Neither
delta resolves the other's hint on the forward path, so `on_progressed` ran
a second, reverse `progressed.resolve_hints(&unresolved)` to close the loop.

Drop it as redundant. Those cycles already clear through the stale-hint
prune of `progressed` against `completed_clocks`, which is the stronger of
the two mechanisms: the reverse pass could only see `unresolved`'s transient
contents, which promotion clears, whereas `completed_clocks` is a durable
per-cohort ledger and so also covers a hint whose resolving commit promoted
through in an earlier cycle.

That ledger is an authority on "this commit is done" because its writes are
gated on promotion: a frontier reaches `ready` only once its own causal
hints have resolved, so a clock recorded there is a commit whose
cross-journal extent was already confirmed. The gating is now written into
its field docs.

The prune itself lifts into `Frontier::prune_hints`, a sibling of
`resolve_hints`. It stays at the `progressed` → `unresolved` handoff,
where it runs against the freshest ledger.

A new test pins the property the mechanism rests on: the prune must apply to
the aggregate `progressed`, and not to the delta which carried a hint. A
hint isn't stale when it arrives — it becomes stale once its commit is
completed elsewhere in the cohort, while it sits in `progressed`.

Resolution becomes single-direction. Visible only in that a resolved hint is
now zeroed rather than left equal to `last_commit`; both are inert, and the
fixtures record the change.

shuffle: ratchet accounted progress into the pending checkpoint

While an unresolved checkpoint waits on causal hints, judge each delta
against the transactional boundary it defines (Frontier::first_unaccounted):
a delta whose every commit and causal hint is already covered — by the
pending frontier's clocks and hints, or by a commit its cohort completed —
is evidence of the current boundary, and is adopted wholesale. The
checkpoint thereby carries the read's true offsets and byte deltas in
place of the conservative -M bump. The first unaccounted delta freezes
the ratchet for the remainder of that unresolved generation.

Idempotent recovery is the primary use case: its one-shot session may
replay a large hinted span, and adoption is the only way its recovery
checkpoint retains the replay's true offsets — so the next session
re-reads only the novel tail, not the whole span.

The fuzz sweep now asserts sweep-wide coverage: recovery cuts never
regress, and at least one replay ratchets strictly forward.

shuffle: horizon-based hint completion, the dual of producer pruning

Shard recovery durably prunes ancient committed-frontier producers, but a
later backfill can re-extract causal hints naming a pruned producer from old
ACKs. Nothing forward-looking resolves such a hint — the hinted journal is
read at its head and the producer is retired — and the per-producer
completed-clock ledger has forgotten it, so the session stalled until
CAUSAL_HINT_RESOLUTION_TIMEOUT and crash-looped forever, each restart
resuming before the hinting ACK.

Bundle the completed-clock ledger with a new per-binding maximum of promoted
read progress into frontier::Completed, and deem any clock trailing that
maximum by PRODUCER_STALENESS_HORIZON completed for the binding. The horizon
is the prune's own clock horizon, moved into shuffle and shared: pruning
guarantees a forgotten producer's largest possible hint trails its journal's
retained group maximum by at least the horizon, so every pruned producer's
hints are dischargeable by construction. Completed applies uniformly at both
prune_hints (which now reports split clear counts on existing DEBUG events)
and first_unaccounted (where the horizon is a third accounting authority,
preventing spurious ratchet freezes over pruned history).

Soundness of the horizon rests on intra-cohort source-clock skew being
bounded far below 48h by the Slice read heap and Log append leveling, both
of which order by priority then adjusted clock. Recovery-seeded hints remain
exempt from pruning, unchanged.

A duality test in runtime-next guards the invariant end-to-end: every
producer actually pruned by prune_committed_frontier yields accounting that
clears its maximal hint.

materialize sync schedule: model, built spec, and validation

Add a model-level sync schedule for materializations: a commit-cadence
control which trades data freshness for reduced destination compute
cost. This is a parallel capability to the connector-config
syncSchedule (which paces by withholding Acknowledged); configuring
both is a build-time error. This commit is dormant under the V1
runtime -- enforcement lands in the next commit.

    syncSchedule:
      baseInterval: 4h              # required
      timezone: America/New_York    # required iff windows are set
      windows:                      # optional, non-overlapping
        - interval: 15m
          start: "09:00"
          end: "17:00"
          days: [Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri]

Model design notes:

- A deliberate clean break from the connector-config field names:
  "interval" values are periods, not "frequencies", and regimes are
  the neutral base/window rather than fast/slow -- a window may be
  slower than its base (e.g. quiet hours).
- baseInterval replaces the connector version's hardcoded 4h slow
  interval and its implicit 30m default: it is required and fully
  configurable.
- Any number of windows, each with its own interval and day mask.
  Windows must not overlap: validation expands each window to weekly
  wall-clock segments (splitting midnight-straddlers) and rejects any
  pairwise intersection; adjacency is allowed.
- The timezone is schedule-level and shared by all windows: per-window
  timezones would make the overlap check undecidable across DST (two
  zones shift relative to each other during the year). Required iff
  windows are configured, rejected otherwise.
- Requiredness is structural (serde-required, in JSON schema
  `required`) rather than custom validation, which retains only what
  schemas can't express: timezone validity, parsed start != end
  ("9:00" == "09:00"), non-empty and non-repeating days, and window
  overlap.
- days is a list of chrono::Weekday (accepts "mon" / "Monday"
  case-insensitively, serializes "Mon"; JsonSchema via schemars'
  chrono04 feature).
- start/end carry a JSON-schema `pattern` which parse_clock matches
  exactly, so the schema and validation cannot disagree.
- models takes the chrono-tz dependency directly so IANA timezone
  names are validated at build time, erroring as early as possible.
  flow-web's wasm32 build is verified OK with it.

Built spec and validation:

- MaterializationSpec carries the schedule as opaque
  sync_schedule_json (field 12).
- The both-places conflict check inspects the connector config without
  decryption (SOPS preserves keys, and schedule fields aren't
  secrets). A cleared-out remnant -- syncSchedule: {} or all
  null/empty values, which the UI's JSONForms editor leaves behind on
  removal -- matches the connector's empty-equals-absent semantics and
  is NOT a conflict, so removal-then-migrate works.

runtime-next: evaluate and enforce sync schedules

Enforce the materialization sync schedule in the V2 leader: when caught
up, the open transaction is held (continuing to combine new documents)
until the next scheduled commit instant.

Evaluation (leader/materialize/sync_schedule.rs):

- The schedule is compiled once at task startup into CompiledSchedule,
  alongside CompiledTriggers. Its fallible constructor re-runs full
  model validation, so a malformed spec fails the task cleanly at
  startup and evaluation itself cannot fail.
- Fires lie on an epoch-relative grid per regime, where the regime at
  any instant is the active window else the base interval. A fire may
  overleap regime transitions, but must not land past the start of any
  FASTER regime: the evaluator walks transitions in (after, fire] and
  clamps to the first where a faster regime takes over, so e.g. a
  short slower blackout window between an overnight regime and the
  daytime base cannot swallow the morning cadence.
- Deterministic jitter spreads load off common grid boundaries: a 24h
  phase hashed from the task's tenant. A tenant's materializations
  typically share destination resources (e.g. one warehouse), so
  scheduling them to commit at coinciding instants wakes that resource
  once, while unrelated tenants spread apart.
- Local-time windows are resolved on the configured zone's calendar:
  enabled days are scanned as local dates (a spring-forward day is 23
  hours, so fixed 24-hour stepping can skip a day outright), window
  exits account for day-mask flips at local midnight, and nonexistent
  local times resolve by bisecting to the end of the DST gap (gaps are
  30 minutes on Lord Howe and 2 hours on Troll station; a fixed
  one-hour step is both non-exhaustive and non-monotone). A year-long
  sweep over pathological zones guards the calendar edge cases.

Close-policy integration: min/max txn duration stay the levers,
varying dynamically rather than being overridden.

- The open-duration band is an evaluate() input: capture and derive
  pass the policy's configured band through, while the materialize FSM
  modulates it per evaluation. While holding, the band collapses onto
  the commit instant -- floor and ceiling alike, so a busy source
  commits exactly on-grid instead of extending past the instant.
  The hold anchors on the transaction's open, not the prior commit,
  which would find an already-elapsed target after any idle gap.
- When no hold applies (a zero-interval regime, or a session's first
  transaction -- never delay the recovery commit), only the schedule's
  floor is waived: the configured max_txn_duration ceiling still
  bounds the transaction.
- The combiner usage ceilings still force early commits, so a backfill
  drains under memory pressure with no caught-up detection; CloseNow
  and graceful stops bypass the floor, so spec updates restart the
  task promptly even mid-hold.

The leader logs the active schedule once at session start, and the
runtime-next README documents the module.

runtime: fix connector container start on non-amd64 hosts

Three defects in the connector container lifecycle, all surfacing as the
same misleading error while QA'ing a local stack on an arm64 host:

    failed to inspect a started docker container (did it crash?)
      docker command ["inspect", ..., "fc_d72959f8"]: no such object

1. `docker run` requests `--platform=linux/amd64` but `docker_pull` didn't.
   Under Docker's containerd image store a platform-less pull fetches only
   the host's variant, so `docker run` found no usable image and re-pulled
   inline. Pass the platform to the pull, via a shared constant.

2. Readiness was signalled by *any* non-empty read of `docker run`'s stderr.
   That inline pull writes "Unable to find image ... locally" first, so we
   inspected a container which did not exist yet and reported a bogus crash
   in place of the real cause on the next line. Wait for the whitespace byte
   `flow-connector-init` writes once its port is bound, forwarding anything
   prior as logs; an un-sent readiness channel now reports that stderr closed
   before the container came up.

3. Container names were `SystemTime::now()` nanos truncated to u32. The clock
   resolves only to the platform timer tick -- 41.67ns on ARM's 24MHz
   architected timer, coarser than the cost of reading it -- so back-to-back
   reads return the identical instant. Concurrent starts (18 at once is
   routine during a build) collided outright, and `docker run --name` rejects
   a duplicate. Use random bits instead.

Fixing (1) then exposed a fourth: plain `docker inspect` reports the *host*
platform's variant, which after a platform-matched pull may not be present
at all, yielding an empty `Config` with no `Created` that fails to parse --
and that JSON is mounted as `/image-inspect.json`, from which connector-init
derives the connector's entrypoint. Only `docker image inspect` accepts
`--platform`; `podman image inspect` has no such flag and needs none, since
it stores the concrete image that `--platform` pulled. Hence the fallback.

local: make stack readiness explicit, and fix two paste-and-see traps

Three findings from QA'ing a local stack, each of which cost real time.

1. Nothing told you when a stack was usable. `local:stack` returned while the
   reactor and sidecar were still in `ExecStartPre` compiling, and
   `flow-plane@<dp>.target` reports active regardless: it aggregates its members
   with `Wants=`, and every unit is `Type=simple`, so systemd marks them active
   the moment ExecStart forks -- before they bind a port. Neither the target nor
   `is-active` is a readiness signal, which leaves hand-rolled systemd polling
   as the only recourse, and it is easy to poll the wrong thing.

   Add `local:stack-wait`: it enumerates this stack's loaded units, maps each to
   the port it listens on, and blocks until all accept connections. It fails
   fast with the unit's journal tail when one enters `failed` rather than
   burning the whole timeout, and names what is outstanding, marking
   `(building)` for units not yet past ExecStartPre. `local:stack` now blocks on
   it before claiming the stack is up.

2. The "ready-to-paste" commands were not paste-able. Both `stack-info` and the
   stack card printed `psql "$FLOW_PG_URL"`, but that variable comes from
   stack-env and exists only under mise. Pasted into a plain shell it expands to
   empty, and psql then falls back to libpq defaults and fails against
   `/var/run/postgresql/.s.PGSQL.5432` -- an error naming neither this stack nor
   the missing variable. `mise exec -- psql "$FLOW_PG_URL"` is no fix: the outer
   shell expands the argument before mise sets anything. Print the URL literally
   instead. flowctl needs only FLOWCTL_PROFILE from the environment, so for it
   `mise exec --` does suffice. AGENTS.md claimed "ambient inside the checkout",
   contradicting its own later note that stack-env applies to what mise runs.

3. `stack-info`'s unit listing dropped the name of any unit that had a problem.
   systemctl prefixes failed/not-found units with a `●` marker, shifting every
   column, so `$1` was the marker and the unit name never printed -- losing
   precisely the unit you needed to see. Pass `--plain`, and surface the LOAD
   column when it isn't `loaded`, which is the signal the marker carried.

Also document connector registration, which publishing requires and which a
present image does not imply. `local/install-connector.sh` already existed, but
was described as an optional helper, while the publish failure it prevents reads
"unknown to Estuary ... reach out to Estuary support for help" -- correct in
production, a dead end locally. The new section quotes that message verbatim so
searching it lands there, and records two things that bite: the image name is
passed without its tag (a separate second argument, defaulting to `local`), and
registration queues a `connector_tags` job that must reach `success` before the
spec schemas validation needs exist.

shuffle: anchor test fixture paths at CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR

Both scenario tests resolved their catalog fixture through a cwd-relative
"./tests/..." path. That works under `cargo test`, which runs from the crate
root, but not when the built test binary is run directly -- and running it
directly is how you exercise signal handling against the test process itself,
such as SIGKILLing it to confirm that spawned etcd and gazette brokers do not
outlive it.

dekaf: stop failing e2e tests on transient data-plane conditions

Two harness bugs accounted for 10 of the 12 test-level failures across the
last six red `Dekaf Test` runs, and for 3 of the 6 job failures outright:

`inject_documents` POSTed as soon as `wait_for_primary` returned, but a shard
reports PRIMARY once its store is ready -- before its connector container is
necessarily running. In that window the proxy can't dial the container and
synthesizes a 503 whose body says "Please retry in a moment"; the harness
bailed instead. The observed gap was ~160ms. Retry for up to 60s, re-resolving
the route each attempt since a container that isn't running may also mean the
shard is moving. Only 503 is retried: it is generated before any request bytes
are forwarded, so nothing was ingested and the POST is safe to replay.

`KafkaConsumer`'s fetch loops returned every librdkafka stream error as fatal,
including `BrokerTransportFailure` -- which librdkafka raises while it is
already reconnecting, and which a real consumer polls straight through. Add an
allowlist of self-healing codes and keep polling, bounded by a deadline so a
broker that never settles still fails. Fatal conditions (bad credentials,
unknown topic) are excluded and still fail fast.

Verified against a clean local stack: 25/25 pass with no nextest retries, while
absorbing two 503s and two GroupCoordinator disconnects that would each
previously have failed a test.

runtime: treat a slow registry as a transient image-pull error

`docker_pull` already retries transient registry failures, but its match list
missed the one that broke a `Dekaf Test` run: Docker's registry client gives up
on a slow registry with `request canceled (Client.Timeout exceeded while
awaiting headers)`, which reads as a client-side error and so fell through to a
hard failure -- surfacing as a publication failure two tests deep.

Applied to both copies of the routine.

ci: bound dekaf-e2e by its own timeout, and dump stack logs on failure

The `dekaf-e2e` profile inherited the default 30s/120s slow-timeout, while
these tests publish specs, wait for shards, and consume through Dekaf. The
slowest have been observed at 81s in CI and 75s locally, which is close enough
to a 120s hard kill to become its own source of flakiness. Give the profile a
60s/300s budget.

Two of the six red runs examined died bringing the stack up, where the
`ci:dekaf-e2e` task's own log dump never runs -- leaving no diagnostics at all
in the run. Add a failure step that captures unit state and journals.

dekaf: retry a group coordinator that isn't servable yet

`connect_to_group_coordinator` built the coordinator's broker URL before
checking the sentinel that says "I have no coordinator for you": an empty
host with a port of -1. Since 35bea4767f8 that URL construction is
fallible, so `-1` failed as `invalid broker port` one line before the
check that exists to handle it, leaving the check unreachable.

Every call site is serving a live consumer-group API, and Dekaf has no
way to hand a client a retryable error mid-session - an error propagates
out of `dispatch_request_frame` and closes the connection, which clients
report as a transport failure. So the transient condition became a
dropped session.

A cluster with no `__consumer_offsets` topic auto-creates it in response
to this very request, so the first consumer group of a cluster's lifetime
reliably hits this. That made it a cold-start race which landed on
whichever e2e test joined a group first, and it is reachable in
production whenever a coordinator is mid-load or mid-election.

Decide the target from the response before touching a URL, honor the
`error_code` the broker sends, and poll while it reports the coordinator
is still loading.

control-plane-api: remove dead evolutions module

`c089b54dc26` removed the evolutions automation once `onIncompatibleSchemaChange` handling moved into the `validation` crate. Two days later `42d0b8b80c1` (`agent-sql` to `control-plane-api`) reintroduced the logic as a byte-for-byte copy of the deleted `agent/src/evolution.rs`, minus the executor wiring. It has had no callers since, and `pub mod` in a library crate keeps rustc's `dead_code` lint from firing on it.

* Remove `control-plane-api/src/evolutions/` and `models/src/evolutions.rs` along with their four cached `.sqlx` queries. These held the last references to `EvolvedCollection`.
* Leave the `evolutions` table, its `create_evolution_task` trigger, and `task_types::EVOLUTIONS` in place. Rows inserted there still enqueue a `TaskType(5)` task that no executor dequeues, and retiring them depends on first cutting the UI's insert path.

protocols: fix dead LambdaConfigJson validation check

`Transform.Validate()` ended its else-if chain with:

    } else if len(m.LambdaConfigJson) == 0 {
        return pb.ExtendContext(err, "missing LambdaConfigJson")

`err` is nil in that branch -- it's bound by the preceding
`else if err := m.PartitionSelector.Validate(); err != nil` clause, which
must have been false to reach here. `ExtendContext` returns its argument
unchanged when it isn't a *ValidationError, so the check returned nil and
a transform with no lambda config passed validation.

Return a new error instead. A sweep of go/protocols found no other
`ExtendContext` call reached from a branch that hadn't just bound a
non-nil err.

This activates a check that has never run, so it's verified against real
specs rather than only unit tests: `mise run ci:catalog-test` passes
37/37 without tripping it, as does the full `go test ./go/...`. Built
derivations always populate the field -- crates/validation derives it
from `model.lambda.to_string()`, which is at minimum "null".

protocols: linked_collections and collection_index for indirected specs

Tasks with tens of thousands of bindings -- up to ~64k, the ceiling that
`doc::combine`'s u16 binding index imposes -- referencing a much smaller
set of distinct collections (~500) replicate a full CollectionSpec per
binding, across built specs, connector requests, internal hops, and
persistence. Add an indirect encoding in which spec-carrying messages
hold a shared `linked_collections` table and their bindings/transforms
reference it by `collection_index` instead of inlining `collection`.

The encoding is a per-message property: non-empty `linked_collections`
means every binding of that message -- active and inactive alike -- uses
`collection_index`; empty means every binding inlines its `collection`,
exactly as today. Mixed forms are invalid. Unique-by-value and
name-ordering of the table are builder conventions, not message
invariants: duplicate names are legal and necessary, since a
materialization binding rewrites its collection's `key` and
`projections[*].is_primary_key` to match `group_by`.

Apply/Open, shuffle.Task, runtime.proto opaque spec bytes, build-DB
blobs, and live_specs.built_spec JSON all inherit for free.

No reader understands the new form yet, so nothing emits it. The
non-proto changes here are the mechanical field additions that exhaustive
struct literals and destructuring patterns require to keep building;
proto-flow's regression snapshots are unchanged, confirming that
inline-form specs remain byte-identical.

Response.Discovered is deliberately left alone: capture discovery has no
CollectionSpec to share, and giving it an indirect form is a separable
change with its own read-side work in the control plane.

protocols: accessors resolving bindings to their collection in either form

Readers of a spec-carrying message shouldn't care whether it inlines a
CollectionSpec per binding or indexes a shared `linked_collections`
table. Add accessors which resolve a binding or transform to its
collection over both forms, so the read-site conversions that follow are
mechanical and form-agnostic.

Rust `proto_flow::linked` adds, for each of flow::CaptureSpec,
flow::MaterializationSpec, flow::collection_spec::Derivation, and the
three Request.Validate types:

- `binding_collection()` (or `transform_collection()`), returning the
  resolved spec *and* its identity: `Some(index)` into the table, or None
  when the binding inlines its own spec and is itself the identity. The
  identity is what a later runtime-next change will key per-collection
  memoization on;
- `resolved_bindings()` / `resolved_inactive_bindings()` / their chain,
  since most call sites iterate.

Resolution returns Option rather than panicking, so call sites keep their
existing `.context("missing collection")` handling. An out-of-bounds index
resolves to None.

Go gains the equivalent `BindingCollection` / `TransformCollection`
methods, and Validate() learns the indirect form natively so that
catalog/build_load.go's Unmarshal-then-Validate flow works for both. A
message with a non-empty table must have every binding leave Collection
zero-valued and its index in bounds; an empty table must have every
binding leave CollectionIndex unset. Each table entry is validated once,
and a materialization binding's FieldSelection is now checked against its
*resolved* collection's projections.

Binding Validate() methods which used to validate their own inlined
collection need the parent's context to resolve, so they're restructured
around unexported helpers; the exported signatures are unchanged and keep
validating the inlined spec, which is what an inline-form binding has.
Inactive bindings are newly checked, but only for agreement with the
message's form -- a no-op for every spec that exists today, and
deliberately not an expansion of what else Validate() inspects.

Nothing writes the indirect form yet, so this is inert.

go: resolve binding collections through accessors in the data plane

Read sites in the Go data plane which reached directly for a binding's or
transform's inlined `Collection` now go through the parent message's
accessor, so they read either encoding transparently.

Purely mechanical: no output changes, as nothing writes indirect form yet.

runtime: resolve binding collections through accessors

Task::new resolves each binding's or transform's collection through the
parent spec's accessor and hands it to Binding::new / Transform::new, which
no longer reach for the embedded field. Harness fixture readers likewise.

No memoization here: V1 runtime gets accessor compatibility only.

runtime-next, shuffle, publisher: resolve collections through accessors

Leader and shard task builders, shuffle Binding construction, and the
capture publisher's binding table all resolve through the parent spec's
accessor rather than the binding's embedded collection.

Builders which destructured the collection out of their binding now take
it as a parameter, resolved by the caller which holds the parent spec.

validation, dekaf, flowctl: resolve collections through accessors

The validation crate's live-binding indices now pair each live binding
with its resolved collection, since a live built spec may be in either
encoding and its bindings are meaningless apart from the spec which
resolves them. Inactive bindings and transforms carried over from the
live spec re-inline that resolved collection rather than copying an index
which means nothing in the spec being built.

`collection_was_reset` takes `Option<&CollectionSpec>` to suit.

Dekaf's `get_binding_for_topic` returns a detached binding, so it inlines
the resolved collection; flowctl preview and fixture readers, the noop
connectors, and the agent test harness use the accessors directly.

derive connectors: resolve transform collections through accessors

derive-sqlite, derive-typescript, and derive-python resolve each
transform's source collection through the parent Validate request or
Derivation, in both the validate and open paths.

This discharges part of the "update key connectors" follow-on: these
three now accept indirect-form requests.

validation: flag-gated writer of indirected collection tables

The builders now construct every built spec and Validate request in
indirect form, interning each binding's collection into a shared table as
the binding is built. The new `indirect-specs` shard flag gates one
contained post-process: when it's unset, the finished message is *inlined*
instead -- each binding re-inlines its collection and the table is dropped
-- reproducing byte-for-byte the encoding which predates indirect specs.

Structuring it this way means the unflagged path round-trips intern ->
inline over every existing fixture, so the unchanged snapshots double as
proof of round-trip fidelity. It also means removal is a deletion: when
indirect form is universal, drop the `indirect_specs` argument and its
branch, and the builder that remains is already the end-state code.

Interning is by value, not by name: two materialization bindings of one
collection whose `group_by` rewrote `key` and `projections` differently are
distinct entries which happen to share a name. Each message gets its own
interner -- a Validate request's table covers active bindings only, while a
built spec's also covers inactive ones, which are re-interned through the
live spec's accessor rather than copying an index across generations.

Inlining is writer-internal. It does not soften the read-side rule that a
spec keeps whichever form it arrived in.

validation, runtime: raise the binding ceiling under `indirect-specs`

`doc::combine::Meta` packs its binding index into a u16, so the combiner and
its spill format hold 65,536 slots. Two independent limits now bound bindings
against it, and they deliberately share no constant:

* `validation::MAX_BINDINGS_INDIRECT_SPECS` (`65,536 - RESERVED_BINDINGS`, 100)
  is the user-facing product gate of a task which sets the `indirect-specs`
  shard flag. Unflagged tasks keep `MAX_BINDINGS` (10,000): every binding of an
  inline-form spec re-inlines its collection, so spec size grows with the
  product of bindings and collection size, whereas indirect form interns each
  collection once and grows only with the binding count. The flag is what makes
  the higher ceiling affordable, so it's also what unlocks it. Either way a
  too-large task fails at publish rather than as a crash-looping shard. The
  reserve exists because the runtime already spends an index on the capture
  connector-state pseudo-binding, and future internal bindings must not move a
  user-visible limit.

* The runtime guards the *format* limit — `bindings.len() > u16::MAX` — early in
  capture `Task::new`, materialize `build_bindings`, `shuffle::Binding::from_task`,
  and the V1 runtime equivalents. At `len == 65,535` the capture pseudo-binding
  at index `len` still fits. The 100-slot reserve is exactly the gap between the
  format limit and the highest validated ceiling, so a validated spec can never
  trip the runtime guard, while the guard still catches hand-built or otherwise
  unvalidated specs.

Without the guard, a spec at exactly 65,536 bindings wraps the pseudo-binding to
index 0 and combines connector checkpoint patches into the first bound
collection's documents — silent corruption. That wrap is unreachable through a
validated publish today and becomes live exactly when the validated ceiling
moves, which is why both halves land together.

The `too_many_bindings` error now formats the limit that was applied, and the
three existing scenarios are unflagged, so their snapshots are unchanged. V1
`crates/runtime` gets the format guard and nothing else: the cliff is in the
shared `doc::combine` path, so it is exposed too.

tests/soak: exercise indirect specs end to end

The soak now carries `indirect-specs` on three of its four tasks, so a
continuously-running workload covers indirect form across all three
spec-carrying task types: `source` (capture, 3 linked collections),
`accounts` (derivation, 3), and `ledger` (materialization, 1 -- its two
bindings of `accounts` intern to a single entry).

docs: clarify BYOK KMS is decrypt-only and identity may not be in dashboard (#3065)

* docs: clarify BYOK KMS needs decrypt-only and identity may not be in dashboard

Two clarifications to the secret-encryption section of the flowctl concept page:

- The data plane identity needs decrypt access only (roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyDecrypter
  on GCP KMS), not encrypt. Estuary only decrypts configs at connector run time.
- Auto-encryption (flowctl and the dashboard) uses Estuary's managed key, so using
  your own key requires encrypting the config manually before publishing.
- For cross-cloud KMS (for example a GCP KMS key with an AWS data plane), the
  identity to grant is not surfaced in the dashboard; contact Estuary support for it.

* docs: make BYOK KMS grant guidance provider-specific (GCP/AWS/Azure)

The grant mechanism differs by provider, so the decrypt-only note now covers all
three: GCP IAM role binding (cryptoKeyDecrypter), AWS key-policy statement
(kms:Decrypt), and Azure Key Vault access policy. Each data plane carries an
identity for all three clouds, so the cross-cloud case is stated explicitly.

shuffle: gate the causal-hint stall timeout on a requested checkpoint

Zero progress is routine while the coordinator is busy and reads are parked
under disk back-pressure, so the timeout could tear down a healthy session
whose connector transaction simply took a long time to store. Count stalled
ticks only while a checkpoint request is outstanding; an unresolvable hint
yields neither a `ready` nor a peek, so its request stays outstanding and the
horizon is still reached.
